utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. May the registrar please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-17/1-T. The Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Furundzija, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The appearances are the same for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the appearances are the same. If I may note something, the computer system here doesn't appear to be working, at least on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can't get the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. We have a blank screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are they still carrying out tests? I am informed it will take a few seconds, so we can just wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judges, may I propose something? Our laptops are showing a simultaneous transcript, so if we're going to go ahead with the direct examination of Dr. Loftus, it will probably take at least 15 minutes, and perhaps the -- well, unless the lights go off, in which case we can go to sleep, I take it, or ... We propose that we go ahead and start with the direct. We can keep track of the transcript and make sure it's accurate from this laptop, and hopefully, within 15 minutes, they can bring us back up to speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. The laptop can show the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Might I just say one thing? I would just like to say that the Prosecution computers now are not functioning either. We will, of course, follow Defence counsel's lead and follow our laptop, but it's very difficult for us, during the direct examination now, to see the transcript of the witness who is being examined also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can see from the laptop?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll move the laptop over so that we are able to follow, but I just want to state that on the screen, where it is more visible, it will be impossible for us also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we can go ahead then, and we shall use the laptops. So the Defence can go ahead and examine their witness. The usher -- can the witness take the oath, make a solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Maybe before we do that, we would like to move into evidence an exhibit. We have talked with the Prosecution about it, and I don't believe they have any objection. It is a medical record taken at the time Mr. Furundzija arrived at the UN detention area. We have a translation. It is in Dutch. There is an English translation that we have. We would like to move them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the Prosecution responds -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I am afraid the technical department says that we can't proceed because they have some serious problems they have to look into, so we shall adjourn until we are informed that we can go ahead. I have to apologise to the witness. Sorry, we have technical problems. We shall resume as soon as everything is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The technical people have informed the Chamber that we can proceed using laptops, and we should all switch off the screens because the repairs are continuing. The bigger screens should be switched off. So we can go ahead using our laptops because the recording will still go ahead. So may the witness please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, as I tried to say before the break, we have some documents that we'd like to move into evidence as Exhibit -- that we're moving into evidence as Exhibit 16 and the translation as 16A. They are a medical record taken by the UN detention unit upon Mr. Furundzija's arrival in custody. They are kept in part of the ordinary course of business in the unit, and it's my understanding, in talking to counsel, that they have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that so, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May the witness make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Would you state your name and spell your last name for the court reporter, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Elizabeth Loftus, and it's L-O-F-T-U-S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Where do you reside, Ms. Loftus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live and work in Seattle, Washington working at the University of Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would like to say that the Prosecution will stipulate that Mrs. Loftus is an expert in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I accept the stipulation, but I would like to just briefly go over a little bit of her qualifications before I go in, and I will cut it down significantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your educational background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beginning with university, I went to the University of California at Los Angeles and I graduated in 1966 with a bachelor's degree in mathematics and also in psychology. Then in 1967, I went to Stanford University. I received a master's -- well, I received my master's from Stanford in 1967, and that was followed by a Ph.D. in psychology in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So you have a doctorate degree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So I should refer to you as "Dr. Loftus"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You may. That would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, since you received your doctorate, what research, if any, have you done in the field of human memory, and particularly the way memory relates to eyewitness testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since receiving my Ph.D. and beginning my academic career, most of which was spent at the University of Washington, I have been involved in literally hundreds and hundreds of studies of human memory, focusing primarily on eyewitness testimony, on people's memories for crimes and accidents, and also on the malleability of memory or distortion of memory that occurs through suggestive influences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: During the course of your career, have you published any books or articles on this subject, and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've published approximately 19 books, approximately 250 or 300 scientific articles and chapters, primarily on the subject of memory. The books actually are on a variety of subjects, but two of the books deal exclusively with the subject of memory, four of the books are on the subject of eyewitness testimony in particular, and then I've also published some textbooks in the area of cognitive psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Loftus, are you at present an officer of any professional organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I belong to a number of professional organisations, including the Western Psychological Association, which covers the Western region of the United States, and I was president of that organisation in, oh, 1984, I think it was. I was also president of a number of other divisions of the American Psychological Association. I am currently a member of the Psychonomic Society, which is the organisation for experimental psychologists, and I served on the governing board of that organisation. At the present, I am a member of the American Psychological Society, I'm a fellow in that society, and I am currently the president of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: During your career, Dr. Loftus, have you received any honorary degrees from any colleges or universities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have received a number of honorary degrees. The first one was in 1982, I believe. I received an honorary doctorate from Miami University which is located in Ohio, in the State of Ohio, and I delivered the commencement address in conjunction with that honour. The second one was awarded in 1990 from Leiden University in the Netherlands. The third one was in 1994, which is a doctor of laws degree, from John Jay College of Criminal Justice, which is one of the universities that is part of the City University of New York system. This college is located in New York State. And then I will receive another honorary doctorate in a few weeks from a British university, from the University of Portsmouth in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: What is your present professional position with the University of Washington?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am a full professor at the University of Washington. My main appointment is in the department of psychology, I am a professor of psychology, but I also have an appointment as adjunct professor of law, so I do have a relationship also with the law school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Loftus, have any of your experiments regarding eyewitness testimony been supported by grants from the United States government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Beginning in the early 1970s, I began to receive support from the US government for my studies of memory and eyewitness testimony and related subjects, and so over the course of the 25 years or so that I have been doing this work, I have been funded by the National Science Foundation, the National Institute of Mental Health, the National Institute of Health, the United States Department of Transportation, and some other agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the nature and type of experiments that you have conducted pursuant to these grants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been the principal investigator of a number of projects, but the ones that are most relevant to eyewitness testimony are projects that supported experiments in which we would, just briefly, present people with simulated crimes or simulated accidents, and then we would test their memory for the details of these events at some later time. One of the major aspects of the situation that I was particularly concerned with in many of my experiments is what happens to memory during that period of time between the crime or accident and someone's statement or recollection of that experience. I studied the extent to which witnesses will respond to suggestions or suggestive information and the extent to which they respond to leading questions or to biased interviews, and the mechanism by which memories can be distorted as a result of suggestion, leading questions, or other intervening activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, before I take you into questions which relate to the case, I want to ask you a question: Are you familiar with the Dusko Tadic case that was tried here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with that case. I pronounce it slightly differently but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: How are you so familiar with that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the case because I consulted with one of the prosecutors on the case, Alan Tieger. There were extensive consultations, at least one long meeting, assisting him with information about that case relevant to the subject of memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Does the fact that you were consulted in the Tadic case in any way pose any conflicts of interest which would preclude you from testifying in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I was first approached about working on this case, I did worry about whether or not there might be some sort of a conflict, just as I would in any case where it looked like the two cases might, in some way, be related to each other, and I thought about this seriously for some time and decided that there were no conflicts in actually working on these two cases in separate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Loftus, have you testified as an expert witness on the issues of memory and eyewitness testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've testified in court cases many, many times, beginning on June 3rd, 1975, my first courtroom testimony; and today, in June of 1998, I've testified perhaps 220 or 230 times in trials of various types.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where the courts were located in which you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primarily I've testified in the United States, although I have testified in some other countries, primarily in the United States. Approximately two-thirds of the cases were criminal cases and perhaps a third, or maybe a little bit more, civil cases. I've testified in State Court, in Federal Court, in military trials, and in other kinds of proceedings, legal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Have you testified for and consulted with the Prosecution in criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, yes. I've consulted with the Prosecution a number of times -- actually, I've only testified one time for the Prosecution in a criminal case, but I've had many engagements with prosecutors over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, in devising experimental techniques for investigating eyewitness testimony, what, if any, categories or subcategories are used with respect to memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very common to think about the field of eyewitness testimony using three categories, and if I might, it might help if I could illustrate this using the ELMO, if that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: The question is, I don't know if the ELMO is working in light of the fact that the monitors aren't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no, because we can't use the screen. Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I'll try to do it without it. The people, the scientists in my field, divide the field into three major stages. In fact, maybe I'll draw for myself and then show it to you when the system is working again, if that's okay? The first stage of the process is called the acquisition stage, and this is a period of time where some event occurs and some information is laid down in memory about that event. In thinking about this particular case, we might be thinking of the event or some events that might have occurred on May 15th, 1993. After the event is over, there is a new phase that is relevant to memory, and that is called the retention phase. Finally, a witness may try to recall information about the event, might answer questions, might make a statement, might try to make an identification of someone who was seen before, and we call that phase the retrieval phase. Of course, we understand that there may actually be multiple retrievals, so if a witness is trying to recall the events that might have occurred on May 15th, 1993, and makes a statement about those experiences on December 7th, 1993, that is an act of retrieval. If there is another attempt to be interviewed or make a statement -- for example, in July of 1995 -- that's a separate act of retrieval. Our job then as scientists in this field is to identify the factors that come into play at each of these phases that affect the accuracy, the completeness, and the confidence of somebody's recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, with respect to the acquisition stage, are there any psychological factors which you have identified in studies that play a role in the acquisition of the information into a person's memory system, and if so, what are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of acquisition or when an event or some events are occurring, there are a number of factors that come into play. Some of them are very obvious factors, such as how good the lighting is or how long a witness has to look at whatever the witness may try to remember later, but some of the factors are not so obvious. Research sometimes shows that they operate in ways that are different from what lay people think is the operation, and I'm talking now about the effects of extreme stress or the effects of experiencing something very violent or the effects of experiencing an event that involves a weapon. These can create a situation that can actually impair memory, especially for peripheral details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you explain the differences to the Trial Chamber, if there are any, between a person's ability to perceive a violent event vis-à-vis a non-violent event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it might help to think about what happens when somebody experiences a violent or highly upsetting event compared to a non-violent event and the kind of studies that have been done to explore this question -- I'll draw this partly for myself in hoping that I might be able to show the court later -- just to give you one example of the kind of study that we have done to look at what happens when people see a very violent event. We might show people a --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, I think the screen is now on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The screen is now working so the ELMO can be operated. Can the usher please assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: As you're drawing, it now can be seen by the Judges and the other lawyers. Go ahead, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one of the studies actually conducted in my own laboratory where we try to look at the effects of witnessing something violent, we showed our subjects a two minute and fifteen second video. The first two minutes show a bank robbery occurring and the last fifteen seconds show a very violent ending in which a little boy is -- the robber is leaving the bank after he's robbed the bank, he is being chased by some employees into the parking lot, and he turns around to shoot at the people who are chasing him -- and this is the violent ending -- he hits a little boy in the face, he shoots the boy. The boy screams and falls over, and this is the violent ending to this event. In this particular study, we took the same film, but we spliced off the ending, the last 15 seconds, and we created a non-violent version. So the beginning two minutes are exactly the same, the robbery happens in the bank and so on, and the endings are different. So one group has experienced a violent ending, the other has experienced a non-violent ending. Finally, we will ask people to recall details about the events. We were particularly interested in the first two minutes of the event, and because these pieces were identical for the two groups, but what we found is that when people tried to recall the details, they were much less accurate in recalling the details if they had seen the violent ending than if they had seen the non-violent ending. So, for example, I'll give you an example of one detail that occurred right here. About two to four seconds before the eruption of the violence, you can see the clothing of the little boy who was shot in the face -- or he was not shot in this version. For example, you might, in one of the studies, I believe about 4 per cent could recall the details of that clothing after they had seen the violent ending, but 28 per cent could recall the details of that clothing if they had seen the non-violent version. We also found that for most of the other details, the appearance of the robber, what the robber said to the bank teller, the note that he handed, for almost all of these other details, people were more accurate if they had seen the non-violent ending. What this violence appears to do is it interferes with the consolidation into memory of these details which would have otherwise been remembered much, much better. So this is an example showing that, experiencing something violent, you can remember what type of event it was, you can remember a few core details about the event, but often the other details are seriously impaired in memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, with respect to a weapon, if a person is threatened with a knife or a gun, does the display of the weapon have any effect on that person's ability to perceive the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In terms of a weapon, yes, and I can illustrate what I mean by that using the ELMO. There is a phenomenon called "weapon focus." There are now a number of studies that have been done on this phenomenon. When a weapon has been used in a crime situation, and the kind of situation that's been simulated might be more like an armed robbery sort of situation, but when a weapon is used in a crime situation, it does tend to capture some of the witness or victim's attention, it leaves less time for looking at other details, it results in sometimes a good memory for the weapon and the description of the weapon, a poor memory for other details that might be going on -- what you might say are "surrounding details." One of the studies that we actually did on the weapon focus phenomenon was to show people -- again, we had two events. One event was an armed robbery that unfolds in a cafeteria type of restaurant where, at some point in time, the suspect pulls out a gun at the cashier -- that would be here, you would see the gun. And in another version, there is no gun, we use a neutral object. He hands her some money or he hands her a cheque, but no gun. While our research subjects were looking at either the weapon version or the no-weapon version, we monitor their eye movements. We hook them up to an eye movement recording device so that we could actually see what they were looking at, we could see the eye fixations and where they were located, and we could even measure how long the eye fixations lasted. Now, if you are a researcher gathering data like this on the fixation patterns that occur with a witness to a scene involving a weapon, one thing you need to know is that when we look around the world and we take in information, whether it's an ordinary event, whether it's a crime, whatever it is, we actually are taking in information in a series of eye fixations. So we make a fixation, and that fixation might last about 250 milliseconds or 300 milliseconds, about a quarter of a second or a third of a second, and then we move to a new location and we make another fixation, and that new fixation is also maybe 300 milliseconds, and we might move to a new fixation or we might fixate again on the same spot. These little jumps between fixations, they last about 40 milliseconds, they're very short jumps, they're called saccades, which is S-A-C-C-A-D-E-S. But the point I want to make is, when we do this research with this technology, we can see a computer display of the scene that the subject is looking at and where exactly a spot of light is moving that tells us where the eye is fixating, and we can actually calculate how many fixations there are on the gun, how many fixations there are on the cheque, and how long those fixations are. When we did this research, we found that when the gun is in the scene, people fixate on it more than they do for the neutral object. Those fixations are actually longer, it might be the difference between an average of 350 milliseconds for the gun and 300 milliseconds for the cheque, and it results in a reduced ability to remember other details, including recognising the face of the person who is holding the weapon. So this is a bit of an elaboration of what we know about weapon focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to the retention period, and, Doctor, are you familiar with the term "retention interval," and if so, would you tell the Trial Chamber what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'd be happy to. I think I will refer back to -- this first graph that I was drawing, it shows an event that may have occurred, for example, on May 15th, 1993. And then there's a retention phase, some period of time after the event until the witness tries to retrieve information about that event. And this is called the retention interval. One thing we know about memory for the event is that it will begin to fade over the course of that retention interval. Now, if we were to then plot a graph of memory, how good the memory is, where this is "good memory" and this is "poorer memory," over the course of the retention interval or the passage of time, you would see typically that memory starts off being relatively good and then it declines. And so as time is passing, the memory is getting weaker and weaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Are you aware, Doctor, of the term "post-event information"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: In the field of memory and eyewitness testimony, does that term, "post-event information," have a specific meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does. "Post-event information," sometimes we even abbreviate it, "PEI," means new information that becomes available to a witness after an event is completely over. That new information can become available to a witness when a witness engages in conversations with other people, when a witness is interrogated about the past, perhaps with the use of leading questions or in a suggestive interview, when the witness sees television coverage about some event that the witness might have experienced. All of these are examples of post-event information that can affect the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment, Doctor. Mr. Davidson, I wonder how helpful this is. Do we need an expert to tell us that memories fade or that if somebody received some information after an event, that it may affect their memory or their recall? I'm concerned about this because we're not a jury and these are all matters which, even for a jury, are matters, I should have thought, are common knowledge and matters which are well within the experience of anybody. And the idea of time being taken up to tell us something we know already, I don't think is very helpful. I wonder, perhaps, if we could move to things which are really outside our experience which the witness can give us evidence about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I moved quickly over the question of memory fading over time. I really want to centre on this question of post-event information and how that relates to the witness's recitation of the events perceived. I would like to move to that quickly and then I will conclude the examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I would like to pose a hypothetical to the witness and give you the following facts and have you discuss those in terms of the question of post-event information. Let us assume that on a date certain, a person is the victim of a violent crime and states that one of the perpetrators is a stranger to her, that is, she hasn't seen that person before or after the date of this violent crime. And assume further that approximately two years later, the victim for the first time describes the assailant as 172 centimetres, blond hair and small features. And then assume further that approximately three years later in trial testimony, the victim describes the person as 180 centimetres with chestnut to black hair. And assume further that between the time of the description of the assailant for the first time two years after the event and before the trial testimony, the witness has seen a photograph on television of the assailant which reflects chestnut to black hair. Now, would the post-event findings and information that you've discussed here today have any relationship to the hypothetical as I have posed it to you? If so, can you explain that to the Trial Chamber, how this information relates to the post-event information about which you previously testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First, it's important to understand about post-event information, that as the memory is fading -- yes, the court is right, that memory fades as a matter of common sense, and you don't need a Ph.D. to realise that. What is not so much a matter of common sense is that as the memory is fading and becoming weaker or whenever there is any other extraneous influence that might be weakening the memory, it becomes more vulnerable to post-event information. So a memory that has been weakened, for example, from 5/15/93 to now six months later, December '93, which is a substantial period of time in and of itself for memory to be decaying, that memory is going to be even more susceptible to post-event influences, to alterations or changes or transformations that are due to some sort of new information or suggestive information that was presented. If you consider the further weakening that might occur as we go into -- a statement, for example, of 1995, and even court testimony from June of 1998, those weaker memories are more susceptible to post-event information. When you see someone's testimony changing so dramatically -- excuse me. I'm looking for the drawing so I can see if it's centred. As in the hypothetical example where we have in July of '95, 172 centimetres, short, blond hair, small features, for example; and now later, you see this dramatic change in testimony to dark hair, 180 centimetres, and so on. One of the most common reasons why a witness's testimony changes from one point in time to another is that that witness has been exposed to some new information, some post-event information. A viewing of the photograph on television in the interval between these two attempts to retrieve information is just the kind of post-event information that we have seen in these studies gets absorbed by a witness and can cause an alteration, a transformation, or the distortion in the memory of a witness who is otherwise trying to be as honest as she can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Loftus, are you familiar with the term "post-traumatic stress disorder"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When someone has experienced a horribly traumatic event, there are sometimes, many times, very serious consequences from that experience. And post-traumatic stress disorder is usually diagnosed when certain symptoms are present, such as depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation or thoughts about suicide, nightmares, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion, Doctor, based on your education and experience in the field of memory and eyewitness testimony as to the relationship between post-traumatic stress disorder and post-event information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do have an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first, it does appear as if there is evidence in this case for a strong reaction to a very horrible set of circumstances and definitely evidence of symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. Now, there has been no explicit study of comparing a PTSD patient's susceptibility to post-event information to a person without PTSD. But based on other considerations, based on the fact that we know that when people are not processing information particularly well, are not able to notice discrepancies between what is being suggested to them and what is part of their memory, and to defend against those discrepancies, under those conditions, people are more susceptible to suggestive influences or to post-even information. In my opinion, this would be a situation where someone would be vulnerable to post-event suggestions and, perhaps, especially vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let me ask you one final question dealing with a hypothetical. Assume that two people are together and both are the victims of a violent event occurring within the same time frame. And assume further that in telling the story of this event, each person tells a version of the event which differs in material ways from the other person's version. Is there anything in the studies and/or your experience which would explain the significant difference in the memories of the two persons with respect to the same event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many reasons why two people can be in the same place and seemingly experiencing the same event and come up with different versions. The obvious reason is that they are paying attention to different aspects of the event. And if they paid better attention to some aspect, their memory might be a little bit better about that aspect. But another key reason why two witnesses can differ so completely is because of post-event information. If one of those witnesses has received some post-event suggestion and has experienced an alteration or a contamination, a distortion in memory, and the other hasn't received that suggestion, then you might very well see two completely different versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have marked the various documents which Dr. Loftus has referred to and drawn during her testimony. I don't recall how many numbers of documents there were, but I think we're on Defence Exhibit 17. I would like to have --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They have been marked Defence Exhibit 17, 18, 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecutor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Since there's been a stipulation with respect to the witness as an expert, I see no reason to clog the record with her curriculum vitae as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that is normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I just ask for a five-minute recess. I would like to just confer with counsel for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The court will take a 20-minute break. There are no more recesses, so we shall start after 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution, please, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Loftus, thank you for your theories on suggested memory. I just have a couple of questions I'd like to ask you. Have you discussed and read with Defence counsel the transcripts of Witness A for this case, her statements from the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, the statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you read the statement from the Investigative Magistrature of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that the July 1995 statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, that's another statement. Have you read that one, Dr. Loftus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read one statement from December 7th, 1993, another from July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you didn't read the other statement from December 1993, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you read her transcripts from previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The transcripts in this proceeding? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you read any transcripts from the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not read transcripts. I skimmed briefly some trial testimony, but I received it much too late to really digest it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand. Have you spoken with the investigators who were involved in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then can I assume that you also have not spoken with any of the investigators that were involved in the statement from Zenica of December 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you have not spoken to any members of the Bosnian War Crimes Commission from the 1993 statement either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I ask you, have you spoken to any of the interpreters who were present when the statement was taken in 1995 by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And have you spoken to any of the interpreters that were present during the rendering of any testimony or transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I ask you, have you been able to look and discuss with Defence counsel the statements of Witness D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review any transcripts that have come from Witness D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you spoken to any investigators involved in the case with Witness D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you spoken to any interpreters that might have assisted during the taking of those transcripts --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- or statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just briefly like to ask you, you understand that the nature of this case, the time frame of this case, is a bit longer than the two minutes that is allotted to some of the your experiences in experiments for eyewitness testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you aware that the time reference in this case spans three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure I understand your question. I understood that May 15th was a critical day for allegations involving one particular defendant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. So then you weren't informed that during a three-day period, one of the witnesses, one of the identification witnesses in this case, had spent that time period at the pertinent place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure who you're referring to, but if you're referring to Witness D, then it's my recollection from the statement I read that his experience might have spanned three days, but I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my question. So then you understand that Witness D was with the alleged accused during this three-day period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that he has, in his statement, various comments about the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you understand that he was with the accused during that three-day period, Dr. Loftus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he was or not, because I was focusing on his recollections about what went on in, I guess what's been referred to as, the pantry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Dr. Loftus, you haven't been informed that there has been recognition, identity of the accused by that witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's my understanding that Witness D knows the accused, served with him in the army and knows who he is, knows his name, and that stranger identification isn't relevant in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, you understand that there has been identification then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Are you also informed that the time period of Witness A is longer than a two-minute span that is similar to the time period in your experiments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly my impression from reviewing her statements that her experiences did span quite a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of when the weapon came out during the incident that involved Witness A?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpreters between the questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. The interpreters would like to have gap between your questioning and the answers of the witness for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A pause?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We're both speaking English and they are interpreting it. I asked were you aware of the -- excuse me. Can I just read back the last question? Were you aware when the weapon came out in the incident with Witness A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my understanding that Witness A was threatened with a weapon, perhaps on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But you don't know how much time passed prior to the weapon coming out in the incident, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You don't know how much time elapsed when the weapon had been produced, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you don't know how much time occurred between the different appearances of the weapon when Witness A was there, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe you often stated or you have testified that there is a core of details that can be remembered during even violent situations, and the peripheral details tend to fade away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, would you say a core detail might be the presence of someone who is interrogating you or threatening you or your children with death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to know whether that is a core detail or a peripheral detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But let's say in an interrogation, would that be a core detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be a person who is threatening you, but it's exactly that kind of -- that is the kind of detail in the weapon focus studies that showed up being impaired when a weapon was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But not when a weapon was not present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only point to the studies themselves that show that even the face of the person holding the weapon was impaired in the studies involving weapon focus. So while it might be considered a central detail, the face of somebody, especially relative to other details, it can still be influenced by the stress and the focus on some objects, some other objects.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Would you agree that prior to a weapon appearing there is no weapon focus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's common sense, I think. Dr. Loftus, I just want to ask you that you cannot state, you cannot testify, that Witness A was mistaken in her identification, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course I can't say whether she was wrong --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- or right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Also, you cannot state, you cannot testify, whether Witness D was mistaken in his identification, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I was commenting on Witness D's identification. Witness D might be accurate in his recounting of who was present at particular episodes, but it is even possible that both of these individuals, who are giving different versions, might have some distortion in their recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But you can't testify that his identity was mistaken, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that my testimony here had much to do with the identification abilities, as far as the defendant goes, of Witness D, since it's my understanding that these two individuals knew each other and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, therefore, you would probably support his identification or his recognition; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to use the distinction that has been used by the Tribunal before, it's recognition rather than identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much, Dr. Loftus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is there any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: None on the part of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Loftus, for giving evidence before the Tribunal. Thank you very much. You are now released. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Defence? Is that the closure of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the Defence rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ready to move on to closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we have then a matter for sentencing. I don't know whether we do that before or after closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, before, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We wanted to make a couple of things -- clarify a couple of points. One, any testimony given as part of a sentencing is not to be used in the case of chief; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I didn't get you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is just purely for sentencing purposes. It is not part of the underlying cases; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which evidence, from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that the next witness is about to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, for sentencing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But not for anything that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, just for sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The second thing is: I disclosed the identity of the witness to Mr. Blaxill at approximately 9.30 this morning. We wanted to avoid a situation where they may need time to investigate the witness, et cetera, after he has already given testimony. And we would like to clarify at this point, if they need a break or a pause before I go into the direct examination to prepare, et cetera -- I anticipate that this examination will not last longer than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, with the clear understanding that this would be an issue of evidence, I understand to be character evidence, that would be considered in the event of conviction as a matter of mitigation, clearly the approach of the Prosecution to the witness would be considerably different as to if it was evidence in chief in relation, in any sense, to the issues of guilt or innocence. We might call or request, Your Honours, for a brief recess if, indeed, anything arises that would require that. I would be thinking in terms of minutes, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: After the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: After the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed. We may not even need to do that, and we may not even cross-examine. I don't know at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It is clearly evidence which will go to sentencing only, not to the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm content with that situation, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May we have the witness brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I want to find out, Madam Registrar, the transcripts are in such a mess. It's not working properly. The sentences are incoherent. Are we still having a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I can advise Your Honours that my screen certainly has gone completely haywire. I'm getting all sorts of nonsense on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But are the laptops okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The laptops are all right, so we'll rely on the laptops, I think. We can proceed. Modern technology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May the witness make the solemn declaration while standing, please? Witness, can you be standing up, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your name for the record? Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does he have the right channel?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Dragan Strbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: In Vitez, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you always lived in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you always lived in the same location in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No. Today I live in the town of Vitez. And until the war, I lived in Dubravica, which is now under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your business or occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Now I work in the sector for civilian defence in the Federal Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know the defendant, Anto Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Anto Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Basically since we were children, since we were born really, because we lived in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where was that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: In Dubravica, in Dubravica, the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know Anto Furundzija's parents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are they still alive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: The mother is still alive and the father was killed in 1993, sometime in August or September. He was killed by the Muslim units as a civilian, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Furundzija's mother lives now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know. She lives as a refugee in a privately owned home in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, does Mr. Furundzija have any brothers or sisters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No brothers. He only has two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How old are his sisters, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: The older sister is three or four years older than Anto, and the younger one is two or three years younger than Anto. I'm not too sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Furundzija ever married and does he have any children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was married and he has a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that a boy or a girl, and do you know the age of that child?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: A girl, approximately three years old, up to three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you were growing up in Dubravica, did you have any occasion to visit in Anto Furundzija's home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did he visit your home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What kind of things did you do together in childhood?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, like all neighbours, we visited each other and we were friends. And as we grew up, you know, I'm a bit older than he is, I played a bit of basketball. I still play basketball. I've been playing for the past 20 years or so. And he started playing basketball since he was very young too, together with me. So most of the time -- we would spend most of our time on sports grounds playing basketball. And after that, I went to university in Zenica, that was in 1984, and at the same time, he started high school in Zenica. So we would see each other every day on the bus to and from Zenica, which means that we spent quite a bit of time together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what was the extent of Mr. Furundzija's formal education?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: A secondary technical school, I think, specialising in transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After school, what, if anything, did Mr. Furundzija do for a living?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: At that time when we graduated, both of us, more or less, at the same time and, of course, in different fields, there weren't any jobs available. So he had to go abroad to make some money, like all young men did. And, of course, young people, particularly, wanted to do this. He went to Switzerland and he spent some time there, and then he returned to Vitez sometime in '91 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long he was in Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, up to a year, about a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When he returned sometime in 1991, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: It was towards the end of 1991. After he came back, the fighting had already broken out, and Slovenia was more or less over. And in Croatia, it had gone pretty far, and Anto joined the Territorial Defence of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge when you knew Mr. Furundzija, did he favour one ethnic group over another? Would you describe him as a nationalist?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Never, by no means. Never did he show, in any way, that he favoured one nationality over another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Anto Furundzija was between October of '92 and October of '94?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Anto joined -- you mean 1992? Anto joined the Croatian Defence Council of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In October of 1994, where were you living at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: In Vitez, in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Anto Furundzija was living at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. He lived with his mother and his family, as I said a few minutes ago, in a briefly owned home as a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Approximately when was the last time you saw Mr. Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, approximately two weeks before he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At any time during your relationship with Mr. Furundzija have you heard anything of a negative nature as to Mr. Furundzija being anything other than an honest and law-abiding citizen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I never heard anything bad about him, nor did I ever have any kind of bad experience when I was in the company of Anto. On the contrary. Anto was an exemplary boy to all, fair, well-liked by his peers, communicative, vivacious, and that's why we all liked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion of Mr. Furundzija with respect to him being an honest and law-abiding citizen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Very honest and fair man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Anto Furundzija has ever been arrested for a crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, if you please, Your Honours, I do have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you say, in 1992, in Vitez, Mr. Furundzija was serving in the TO, the Territorial Defence, did you enter any military service at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Not military service. Since 1991, I have been working as the head of the Department for Civilian Defence in the municipality of Vitez where I stayed throughout; that is to say, throughout all the fighting in 1993 and 1994. And then, in 1994, I continued to work as the head of the Department for Civilian Defence in the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior; and then in '96, yes, that's right, in 1996, I was transferred to the Ministry of Defence as head of department, and now I work as an associate in the field of civilian defence in the Federal Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have said that Mr. Furundzija was in no way a nationalist, but is it not correct that he changed sides from the TO, of the government Territorial Defence, and then joined the HVO, which was, I understand, a nationalist movement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that the HVO is a nationalist movement. On the contrary. At that time, joining the Territorial Defence only shows that Anto was not of a nationalist orientation at that time because at least at that time the Territorial Defence was an institution which brought together all nationalities, all ethnic groups. So because of his very own position and views, Anto joined that group. But due to general developments in Vitez, Anto was probably compelled to change from one component to another in 1992. I believe that Anto did not do this because he believed that the HVO was above the Territorial Defence. It is the events themselves, political and military events, that were occurring at the time, probably forced him to do so. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the unit "the Jokers"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that they had a reputation of being certainly very tough and resourceful soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I can't really say what kind of reputation they enjoyed. It was a special unit. I don't know what kind of reputation they had, at least I'm not in a position to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say then that you have no direct knowledge of the activities of the Jokers or Mr. Furundzija whilst he served with them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, because I was so busy on my own in the field of civilian defence and taking care of civilians in general, that our activities were really separate from one another, so I didn't have any opportunity to be in contact with the Jokers or any other military units because I was dealing with problems related to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have nothing further. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We'd ask that the witness be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give evidence. You are now released. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are the parties ready for closing arguments? Have you closed your case for the sentencing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honours. I believe we closed before the sentencing evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before this one, just one witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we have closed the sentencing evidence now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Are we ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There was just one point, Your Honours. Certainly, if the court desired, we are in a position to make certain comments regarding the issue of sentencing, matters of principle or from the rules or from previous jurisprudence in the Tribunal, but we have no intention of calling evidence in respect of sentencing. So if that helps the court in scheduling the way forward, that might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean you would make your general comments as part of your closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In essence, although my co-counsel and I have divided that duty between us and the sentencing issue, I would ask leave to address you, but it is very brief and it, as I say, involves no evidence. Unless you would -- sorry, Your Honours. I was going to say, unless you would like me to commence with that and join it to what has just gone on, as we move into that mode?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It is up to you how you arrange it, whichever, because they are separate parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed. But as the sentencing exercise has proceeded in respect of that part for the Defence, I am quite happy to make the observations for the record now. Then my learned friend can close for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: As I've indicated to Your Honours, there is no proposal by the Prosecution to call evidence in relation to sentencing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speaker please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Louder and slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the gravity of the crime if proven and a conviction ensues, the Prosecution simply refer Your Honours, with respect, to the evidence essentially of Witnesses A and D. I think that covers all issues of gravity. The status of an accused is a matter that has raised itself and is one you will be able to resolve from the issues as to his seniority and relative time served and status as a soldier, which would impact, of course, on his personal conduct in terms of the degree to which, although ignorance is no defence, one's experience is something that obviously influences the degree to which you should be familiar with the laws of war that apply to your conduct and your duties. I will move on, Your Honours, very briefly to the effects and the factors in Rule 101 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and 101B, wherein particularly the Trial Chamber may take account of such factors as aggravating circumstances; mitigating circumstances, including substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor before or after conviction by the person concerned; the general prison sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia, and any sentence served that has been imposed by a State court arising from a conviction for the same act, and this reflects essentially also Article 24 of the Statute of the Tribunal regarding penalties. Your Honours, if I can examine these in brief? Firstly, the gravity of the offence in terms of aggravating circumstances. Of course, the offence of torture in itself is a serious offence, and where this involves, at its basis, serious mental or physical suffering, one would then rely upon the facts as to the extremities of that suffering to give an indication, both in terms of duration and the nature of the acts, as to the gravity. The Prosecution would say that if all stands proven at the end of the day, this goes to the heavier end of gravity for an offence of torture. As for outrages upon personal dignity, again, perhaps if the allegations at the end of the day stand that rape is involved here, we have probably the most severe form of outrage upon personal dignity, and the physical, personal, and sexual integrity of the victim. The aggravating circumstances might well be that not only the nature and gravity of the acts perpetrated but the very fact of the presence of others, other soldiers present during virtually the entirety, indeed the entirety of the events of that day, and the fact of allowing, as the Prosecution have alleged, another, encouraging, aiding and abetting another to behave towards the detained victim to the level of a series of rapes, is a serious aggravating dimension. With regard to mitigating circumstances, clearly, Your Honours, the Prosecution's submission is that there would be none. Mitigation requires, in any event, some expression of contrition, it would possibly be a mitigation if there be a plea of guilty. There are other mitigating factors, but when one clearly fights a case to its conclusion on the basis of not guilty, the question at that stage of mitigation is, I respectfully suggest, not relevant -- or not applicable, I would say. With regard to the sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia, I am not aware of any particular sentencing passed in the courts of that country, or now those countries, in relation to an offence of this nature, but I suffice it to say, by reference to the decisions in the Tadic case in the sentencing judgement, that the most directly applicable provisions of the former Yugoslavia appeared to be in Chapter 16 of the SFRY penal code. Therein, under the titles "Crimes Against Peace and International Law," there are provisions relating to sentence for crimes involving killings, tortures, inhumane treatment of civilian population, causing great suffering or serious bodily injury to body or health, amongst other crimes. Discussed by the Tadic Chamber, Your Honours, the Article 3 crimes had been linked to that particular Article of the penal code due to the common relationship between Common Article 3 running across the Geneva Conventions, since Article 142 had specific applications to the Geneva Conventions. Let us say the commencing parameters within that Article are quite wide. Under the laws of Article 142, the reality is that such a crime shall be punished by "no less than five years' strict imprisonment or by the death penalty," since that remedy still appertains in that former jurisdiction. Clearly, the latter is totally inapplicable within the remit of this Tribunal and rightly so, but it does indicate that at the top end of such sentencing, within the scope of that Article of the SFRY penal code, the reality is that, as it were, the maximum is a potential option to the court. As regards anything else, the Prosecution would say that we are not at this time possessed of any specific information as to the detriment of the character of Mr. Furundzija in terms of any previous convictions. No such information is to hand. I would simply then advise you, of course, at the end of the day, take into account time served, and would just simply remind the Honourable Chamber that Mr. Furundzija came into custody on the 18th of December, 1997. Those are the only representations I propose to put before Your Honours in relation to the issue of sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The other part?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then we will proceed to our closing argument?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to say good morning again, Your Honours. This trial has been historical, not because of the, come now, what will be known as the shortest trial before an International Tribunal, nor because it has been the most complex in terms of political or military strategy or analysis, but the case of the Prosecutor versus Anto Furundzija, which is before this Honourable Trial Chamber, is an important case within the mandate of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. This case will bring justice to persons, particularly in this case a woman, who was caught in the cruel conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Your Honours, I would remind you, although I think one need not be reminded, that this case calls the simple rendering of justice. Simple justice, as Thurgood Marshall used to say, but in our instance would be for the violation of the laws and customs of war, particularly that were committed in the Lasva Valley, or more specifically at the Joker headquarters on or about May 15th, 1993. The Prosecutor has submitted witness testimony that, in our view, proves beyond a reasonable doubt that Anto Furundzija should be found guilty of torture, outrages upon personal dignity, including rapes, as prohibited by Article 3 of the Statute. The evidence assuredly ushers no other conclusion. The basis of the present case, some very fundamental features and facts, and I would say legal constructs, have been uncontested by the Defence. The Prosecution led evidence that proves the existence of an armed conflict. The armed conflict occurred between the Croatian Defence Council, which we have commonly referred to as the HVO, and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the municipality of Vitez, and this all occurred during the time period of the alleged crimes. During that armed conflict, civilians were killed, houses were burned, and families were forced to flee. On or about the morning, but one can say here specifically the morning of April 16th, 1993, Anto Furundzija, a member of the Joker unit of the HVO, together with other armed and uniformed soldiers, entered Ahmici, part of the Vitez municipality, and participated in that armed conflict. The record will show that Anto Furundzija's military responsibility that day concerned the expulsion of a former female classmate and her mother. They were both Muslims. They were told, forced at gun point, to leave their homes. That witness has clearly identified Anto Furundzija. She was a former classmate who pleaded with the accused, while he stood in stoney silence, not to leave her home. Her evidence was wholly credible, uncontested by the Defence. The testimony of Dr. Mujezinovic, former member of the crisis staff and former president of the Bosnian war presidency, described the length and, finally, the process of negotiation in settlement of the armed conflict. He also described an armed conflict that did inflict death, detention, expulsions, rapes, and terrorisation of the Muslim population in the Lasva Valley. He assessed this conflict from the power take-over in 1992 to the full-blown war in 1993, and finally, what was called the cessation of hostilities that occurred in 1995. Anto Furundzija took part in this conflict. Prosecution witnesses, such as Dr. Mujezinovic, Witness B, Witness C, Mr. Kavazovic, testified about the existence of this conflict, and the active participation within the HVO of a special unit or force called the Jokers. Members of this unit were wounded in conflict; they were taken to the hospital where Dr. Mujezinovic was ordered to work. The Jokers were part of the armed forces that searched apartment buildings, particularly those apartments of Muslims. The Jokers arrested and detained, interrogated other members of the HVO and the Muslim population. The Jokers transported and forced civilians to dig trenches near the front-line. They formed part of the ominous military presence in the city of Vitez. The very name appeared to instil fear, according to our testimony, within the Muslim population. The unit obtained a notoriety. The stories centred on their headquarters often, a place called "the Bungalow," generally referred to as a bungalow because it used to be a restaurant. Now it had become a military headquarters. And Anto Furundzija was a recognised member of the Jokers. This evidence has been uncontested, Your Honours. We would state that the Prosecution has entered ample testimony and proof beyond a reasonable doubt of what we call these foundational measures. Then on or about May 15, and it was pleaded "on or about May 15th, 1993," the evidence shows that Witness A was arrested, detained, and transported to the Bungalow. Now, I would like to say one word about the time factor. As pleaded in "on or about," the Defence would make us think that these events did not occur on May 15th. We would readily agree. Maybe they didn't occur on May 15th. But for the Defence to put forward evidence to say that, due to the date the events did not occur, is wholly incredulous. The Defence cannot raise any inference that the crimes did not occur, and certainly the Defence, up until this point in time, has not raised any evidence or presented to us the existence of an alibi that the events did not occur or they did occur but that the accused was not present. So, therefore, during this time period, the evidence shows that Witness A was arrested, taken to Nadioci where the former restaurant known as "the Bungalow" stands. Only now, it is the headquarters compound of the Joker unit. Now, Witness A testified that she was removed from her car and led by a uniformed Joker past the main building; she was taken directly to the sleeping quarters of the Joker headquarters. The room was filled with beds and bunks, and there were roughly maybe about 40 uniformed and armed members of the special HVO forces, the Jokers, there.
