Now, it is important to note that the Joker member did not need to inquire or stop in the main building. He knew he was to lead Witness A directly to the barracks, knowing that she was to be arrested, brought not to the main building, taken to the sleeping headquarters, the barracks, of the Joker unit, and told to wait. And then, Your Honours, I would submit the tragedy really began. Now, one might want to look at this almost as if it were theatrical, but it is tragedy nonetheless. We have Anto Furundzija, who is the director and the actor, and although he is not always present on the scene, might I just show you what the evidence has shown within this Trial Chamber? Witness A was told to wait. While waiting, the Joker members who surrounded her mentioned that "the boss" was coming, then started saying the name "Furundzija," and the accused, duly identified in court, appears. He begins by saying, "Now, lady, interrogation." But he knew she was there, he knew she had been arrested, he knew what he was going to interrogate her about, and he knew the other Jokers were in the room. So he began the interrogation. He controlled the dialogue. He offered threats against her sons, threatened to kill them. He didn't encourage her to tell the truth. He threatened what would happen if she didn't tell the truth. There came a time period during this interrogation that Witness A was forced to remove all of her clothes and to remain nude during the controlled questioning. The unrehearsed victim at this point was subjected to a knife --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honours. Our computers are now completely down. Apparently it's mine then. If someone could assist me here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Aren't the laptops working?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll look on with Mr. Davidson so we don't have a pause here, but if they could perhaps come and try to fix it in the meantime? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we can proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As I stated, the knife was rubbed up and down Witness A's body by another member of the Joker unit when the accused Anto Furundzija was not only present but was still saying his lines, still interrogating. What was the reason for the knife? What was the reason for such a physical threat during the interrogation after the mental threats, threats to kill one's sons, had occurred? The witness testified, Witness A, that the person who held the knife threatened to cut out her vagina, a threat of a bodily sexual mutilation, during the questioning by Anto Furundzija. There has been testimony too that the witness, in this nude state, among the other Jokers, was forced to dance. I would ask the court to look at the public in this tragedy, theatrical display, the other Jokers who were around. It was not an innocent or naive or incidental public, they were members of a group who very well understood, when one of their Joker members conducted an interrogation with a forced nude Muslim woman with threats of death and mutilation before them, that this was a strong, strong interrogator. This was a serious unit. This interrogation is held in a bedroom barracks. The intensity of the questioning, the intensity of the other acts that were performed, the admissible sexual assault evidence that the court will allow in at this point concerning Witness A, could only have been intentionally caused, and did cause mental, severe mental suffering, as required under torture. Then there is testimony that the accused left in disgust. But was he disgusted at the humiliation, the degradation? No, it appears that he was disgusted at the lack of the unrehearsed victim to participate with the correct answers, with the truth in his interrogation. So the record shows that he left and that Witness A remained with whom I will refer to, and I think this is a title given by learned counsel before, let's say "Accused B." Now, when Anto Furundzija left the room, he certainly had seen everything that occurred in the room prior to leaving. He certainly knew that Witness A remained in the room forcibly naked, forcibly frightened. He probably could also understand that her

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: necessarily a situation in which she would find comfort. He had been present. He had seen. He had controlled the first part, and I would allege this is the first part of the interrogation. But Anto Furundzija had other things to do. Anto Furundzija was not getting the answers that he wanted from this victim. How dare she? Well, we can continue. Let's go to the second act. The director moved offstage. Other actors continued. And then word was sent, and the transcript does show that another soldier came in and then

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: told them, and they followed the instruction, both of them, "Let's move over to the pantry." Now, what I should explain is happening and what the record clearly shows is that during this time period and before this time period, we have another unrehearsed victim, but let's say "witness," Witness D, who, during a three-day period, has been arrested and detained by the Joker unit in the Bungalow. Jokers do do this. The evidence also shows that while he was detained, the accused, who he readily could identify, was at the Bungalow while he was being interrogated, let's say "debriefed," concerning a prior stay with the Muslim army. Witness D had been in the hands of the Muslim army and then, soon upon his release, was arrested by the Jokers to find out whether anything had been said about the Jokers to the Muslims. But he wasn't the only one there. Even the Defence produced a witness that showed the same scenario: Arrested by the Muslim army, then picked up by the Jokers, taken to the Bungalow to be "debriefed," to give a statement. The only difference between the two witnesses -- and I would allege that there are some differences -- is that Witness E from the Defence came in, obviously wrote his statement or agreed with the statement, whereas Witness D, Witness E says, wrote a statement, but they wanted Witness D for something else. Maybe he could participate a bit further. So during a three-day period, Witness D is held within the Joker compound and brutally beaten on his body and beaten around the head. Even Witness E will say that, "Yes, we saw a bottle smashed

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: time period, beat him up." I understand that Witness E might not have given all of the details that even Witness E witnessed, because at that time period he was busy for 35 minutes filling out his statement, and during the other 18 hours, while he stayed awake the whole time, I imagine he wasn't in a position to see, or maybe Accused B is not someone to be tangled with. I think Witness D would certainly understand

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: intentionally inflicted mental and physical harm, a person who had a reputation, who was known, particularly among that Joker unit within that Bungalow, within that compound, with people who came outside and who were not Jokers, that this was a person who inflicted mental and physical pain. So let's go back to our scenario. Anto Furundzija has left the first part of a two-part continuing interrogation rather disgusted at the witness, the victim, went back, and who does he now bring into the scene? Witness D. But why bring in Witness D when you're trying to get information from Witness A about her sons or about other members of the Croatian army? Because Witness D is a member of the HVO who had guarded the house of Witness A. He is confronted, delivered by Anto Furundzija because Witness A must speak. Now, as Anto Furundzija leads Witness B back to what is referred to as the pantry, and, yes, there might be differences in how one entered the building and there might be differences about the light being on or the light not being on, there is absolutely no disputed evidence that Anto Furundzija did not go get Witness D and lead him to the pantry to confront Witness A. He knew Witness A would be in the pantry because he had already sent someone to have her moved there. He knew that Accused B would be in the pantry. The person came in and said, "We're moving over." So therefore, he went directly to the pantry with Witness D and said something to the effect, "Now let's see who will talk, who will confess." He was not surprised to see Witness A continued in a state of nudity covered by a blanket. He was not surprised to see Accused B. He certainly wasn't surprised to see the condition of Witness D. He returned to his role of interrogator, and Witness A clearly hears the continuation of the questions. Is she focused on him and was she focused on him in the first room? I believe she was. This was the person who controlled her life and her death, who controlled the other Jokers, who controlled the scenario. Did she recognise him in the second room? Even if we believe that the room was dark, that she didn't get a chance to look at him, would she forget that voice that within that very day had threatened to take away what is possibly the most precious things she has during this war, her two army-aged sons? But I don't think that we even have to necessarily pry into that too much because we have Witness D who has been with the accused for three days, who readily just recounts, "Yes, I was taken to the pantry by Anto Furundzija," and, once again, we have the interrogation verbally which is combined with the acts. Now, it is very interesting that I find that three witnesses, one called by the Defence, two called by the Prosecution, one a witness who I think the court understands was not a ready witness but who did come to testify. I'm referring to Witness D. They all describe the exact same manner of the beating that occurred in the second room. These witnesses had no contact. I have no information that Witness E contacted Witness D subsequent to these events. And there has been testimony that there's been absolutely no contact between Witness A and D. They didn't even know whether the other were still alive. But the beating of the feet from the top, not the soles, which most people might think is common, but they call describe the manner in which the feet were beat. Maybe it's a Joker technique, but it's a technique that occurred in the pantry on that day. And then, because Witness A still didn't please the interrogator, Anto Furundzija, Accused B started to sexually assault her. What was the nature of the sexual assaults? Your Honour, we would say that they were rape under international law, that they were the forcible sexual penetration of Witness A's vagina, her mouth. She was asked to swallow the sperm of Accused B. She was asked to lick his penis after there was anal intercourse or faeces were on it. And this was done because "You don't beat women. We have other means of making them talk." But who wanted them to speak? Who wanted the information? Who was the principal director and actor? Now, the testimony seems to show, at this point in time, Witness D is continuing to be beat on the feet, maybe around the head, but then Witness D testifies that he is brought over and forced to watch the rapes and other sexual abuse of Witness A. And then the question arises: Where is the interrogator? Where is Anto Furundzija? Is he in the room? Is he outside the door? Has he left but stayed around? His presence is there and is felt. It's his play. He is in control of the entire theme, whether he steps out to take a cigarette, to talk with his public, which is still around, of Jokers clambering around the door, or whether he is inside interrogating. There is no alibi. There is no other place he was at this time. Anto Furundzija was continuing, what we will call, the common scheme of the interrogation, of torture under international law. I would just like to go back a moment to the public. The public followed the play. They might have left the larger room soon after Anto Furundzija left, but they, again, showed up when Furundzija transported forcibly Witness D. And it appears from the testimony that they stayed around, because when Witness D recalls being taken out, he has testified that he still heard cries and screams of a woman. The only evidence we have that day of a woman being present at the Bungalow and in the direction of the cries and screams appears to be Witness A. And then he heard the Joker men saying or shouting or chanting, "Furundzija, Furundzija." Now, I will grant you that there is evidence that there were two Antons that day or within the Jokers. There appeared to be only one Furundzija. There appeared to be only one Furundzija who was the leader of the Jokers or looked upon as someone with the status of leader. And there appears that only that one Furundzija, as far as the testimony has shown, was present in the pantry or in the first room. Now, Your Honours, what I would suggest, but I think it's just far too obvious, but please allow me to say it, there is no expert testimony that's necessary or needed here. Witness D recognised the accused Anto Furundzija. He had been with him for three days. He had been arrested, detained interrogated by the Joker unit and Anto Furundzija. Witness A identified Anto Furundzija. And what the court will see in reviewing the documents and exhibits in this case is that she has never said it was anyone different. She has never elaborated or detracted upon the role of Anto Furundzija, has never said that "He tried to touch me," has never invented to make him more of a physical perpetrator or more horrible, because Anto Furundzija's acts were criminal and horrible enough in and of themselves, the principal interrogator, the principal torturer. Witness A has remained consistent throughout the five years on that issue. Witness D certainly corroborates that. At the close of our pantry scene, we run into a little bit of difficulty. When did the scene end for Witness D and when did it end for Witness A? How long was Anto Furundzija at that pantry? I would and I must say that the accused staged, executed, committed, in the very, very least, aided and abetted in the commission of crimes under our Statute. I would like to go into the criminal allegations, and then I'll briefly terminate with Article 7(1). I believe the evidence has shown clearly that we are talking about the crime of torture, the intentional infliction of severe mental pain or suffering upon a victim. In this instance, it's important to see that this torture was related to the armed conflict. She wasn't brought in to find out who her sons were dating. She was brought in for information that would be of assistance, if not dire use, to the HVO, concerning the relationships of HVO persons with Muslims during a war; persons such as Zlatko Nakic, information about what occurred in the buildings where they were holding Muslims in the basement, information about Vlatko Males, information about other Muslims who lived in the building. This interrogation was related to Anto Furundzija's function during the war, and that's why he was intent upon getting that information. He wanted it from the side of Witness D and, certainly insistently, from the side of Witness A. He intentionally, under torture, intentionally inflicted serious mental pain and suffering on Witness A for that information. And when she didn't give it, he intentionally inflicted serious mental pain and suffering to punish her or to intimidate her, but he was going to have the information. Now, under torture law as proposed by the Prosecutor, and as this honourable Trial Chamber will be able to adjudicate for one of the first times in international law, you know that you have to have the acquiescence or consent of an official. There appears to be no doubt that Anto Furundzija was an official within the Jokers. The Jokers were an official unit within the HVO. And the HVO is, without a doubt, one side of the armed conflict. I believe that the Prosecutor has presented and proved beyond a reasonable doubt the elements that are required for torture. In terms of Furundzija's intention, one need look no further than the threat to kill, the forced nudity, the threat of mutilation, the continuance of an interrogation that has, up until a point in time, been filled with violence. All of the admissible sexual evidence from the first room and certainly all of the sexual evidence from the pantry, the rapes, the sexual abuse, particularly the degrading manner in which the forcible sexual penetrations were carried out, show that he intended to inflict serious mental harm and commit the crime of torture as an official representative of the Jokers and the HVO army. The evidence concerning outrages upon personal dignity. If the court were just to look at outrages that were separate from rape, we would still have forced nudity in a public venue, in the meaning that it was not in Anto Furundzija's small office in the Bungalow, if he had one. It was in front of the Joker men who were armed. All of the acts took place in this type of public setting in the hands of, from the point of view of Witness A, the enemy. Personal integrity. "Take off your clothes. Your vagina might be cut out." Sexual integrity. Well, it's hard to unpeel, it's hard to say when one did not blend into the other at this point due to the method of this interrogation. When we move to the pantry, we have a continuation of outrages upon personal dignity, but taken to another level with the forcible sexual penetrations, and then having Witness D forced to witness the rapes of Accused B upon Witness A while Witness A knows that this is someone who has helped her sons. This is someone who the Jokers have no qualms about beating and forcing him to see such degradation and rapes. What was the fear that must have gone through her mind and body? Outrages upon personal dignity, which includes our sexual integrity and which, in this instance, undoubtedly included multiple, multiple forcible sexual penetrations or rapes. The evidence of rape I've already gone over. I think there's absolutely no question that these rapes were done intentionally. I think the common scheme of the interrogation was almost like one intentional act, but one still has to link the accused to the crimes. What is his individual, criminal responsibility? Well, I believe certainly, certainly for the torture, the Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that he committed the torture. There's evidence of planning and setting the scene, but he certainly committed the torture. The Prosecution would emphasise the commission, although Your Honours might find otherwise. In terms of outrages upon personal dignity, I think that when you're in the hands of a detained -- when you're a detained person in the hands of another power under Article 3, there is case law that says there could be a duty to that detained person to make sure that person is not ill-treated or molested or that anything should occur to them. Well, it certainly has been noted in case law, particularly, the "Essen Lynching" case when the German police turned over to a part of the German army three British military pilots, and Erich Heyer stated to his sergeant, "We'll take them for interrogation down the street," but the meaning was very well understood, "We will march them through this angry crowd." And those three British pilots did not make it through the angry crowd. The crowd killed them. And Erich Heyer was found guilty, even though he never touched them, but he initiated, and the court does talk about that it was impossible to separate out the acts, that Heyer admittedly never struck a physical blow. His part was entirely verbal. But in knowing that these British soldiers would be marched through a crowd where there was little likelihood of survival, the court found that he did not uphold a duty to detained persons who were in his hands, and that, in essence, that was a violation of the Laws and Customs of War. Even the sergeant, who stood nearby and escorted the men and never interfered with the crowds' brutal interference with the prisoners of war, was found guilty and sentenced to five years. I would say that the outrages upon personal dignity, and the court might also find the rapes, that Anto Furundzija certainly didn't fulfil any duty to a detained person in his hands, even if he never touched the person once. But the court might also find under 7(1) that Anto Furundzija aided and abetted in the rapes. Now, with aiding and abetting, one has to be directly a contributor and/or merely more -- pardon me, more than merely present. I think that the court can certainly look at a direct contributor through the lens of omissions, of omissions of acts, even if we put aside the acts of threat, the acts of knowing that Accused B would rape Witness A in the pantry. There was no move to stop that. There was no move just to say, "I will complete my interrogation at the Bungalow." There was no move to say, "This woman will not speak. I've finish my interrogation," more or less a move to tell anyone to stop what was clearly illegal under law, and that would be raping during an interrogation. There was neither an act of salvation, and we cannot count the omissions that were committed. As a matter of fact, in terms of aiding and abetting, the presence of Anto Furundzija, whether it was insertedly next to her, near the door, milling around with his men, had an encouraging effect on the commission of the rapes. It gave out the silent signal or maybe not so silent. Everyone understood. It's very interesting that this Tribunal, in their first case that has come to a judgement, the Prosecutor versus Tadic, had to look at what I would call an analogous, if not a similar, issue. That was the issue of Mr. Tadic, a man who did not have the military affiliation that Anto Furundzija has, who was with a group of guards in a second setting, after having been actively participating with the guards in previous settings of types of abuse and brutality. And in the second setting, it appears that Mr. Tadic, in the Omarska camp, was present while one guard sexually -- I'm sorry, one inmate was forced to sexually mutilate another inmate. Now, the court found that Mr. Tadic was not merely present, that his presence has an encouraging effect, even though in this second incident, he had not said one word; he had not touched one inmate. Our facts are much stronger, much clearer, and it's much more evident that there was no mere presence of Anto Furundzija during the entire interrogation, nor during the second part in the pantry. He participated by bringing "D," by verbally starting this second phase of the interrogation, and by having a presence during the commission of the sexual assaults, the repeated rapes. Now, this Tribunal has seen fit to look at such law and pronounce a judgement, such as Tadic, by saying that those acts and omissions incur liability under Article 7(1) of our Statute. Your Honours, I would just like to conclude by briefly looking at questions of credibility of the witnesses. The Prosecution has called Dr. Mujezinovic, a man whose relationship to these matters, in many ways, is quite formal. It has to do with positions he held within the Bosnian war presidency and, prior to that, during the crisis staff. The relationship that he might have to Victim A is minimal, if relevant at all. I believe his testimony was credible and was mainly centred on issues of the existence of the armed conflict politically and its various manifestations. The court heard Witness B. Witness B, as the court very correctly stated, is not related to the criminal acts of this trial, but her testimony, that of a woman who was betrayed by a friend in stony silence while she was being expelled from her house at gun point, was credible. There is no reason that I believe the Chamber can detract from any of her testimony. Then we have Witness C. Witness C recounted what it was like to live in Vitez during the time period of the armed conflict. In some ways, other than the arrest and detention, her story parallels that of Witness A. I believe the testimony was factually accurate and credible. Then we come to the testimony of Witness D, as we stated before, somewhat of a reluctant witness, did not want to disturb the peaceful state in which he has finally found himself after the years of armed conflict. It's a witness that was attractive, to a certain extent, for both sides, both the Defence and the Prosecutors. He was a witness who came and stuck to what he saw and what happened to him. I think the court could certainly see that this was not a witness that exaggerated on one side or on the other. He testified truthfully, down the middle. But what was pertinent, I think, to his testimony was the physical reaction that his own body had to the testimony. I don't know if it was perceived by the Chamber, but it was quite obvious that Witness D's body could not stop rocking back and forth every time he spoke about the beatings that had occurred at the Bungalow. His shirt just started flapping. But he maintained his testimony, and I believe it was the testimony that, in the main points, were very, very credible. I believe that Witness D rendered a service to this Tribunal by coming. We have Witness A. Witness A, similar to many victims of armed conflict, has a horrible story to tell, hers, perhaps, as, if not more, horrible than that of many persons, particularly, many women, in the former Yugoslavia. Witness A came, she spoke. In the opening statement of Defence counsel, we were warned, "She will be a very sympathetic witness. Everyone will like her. Horrible things have happened to her, but she is just not remembering correctly, and let's not have that cloud our understanding of the case." I think Witness A has shown the proposition to be true that many people who have been sexually assaulted and particularly violated, the problem is not remembering; the problem is forgetting. She came, she remembered. The gist of her story, the core of her story, if we want to use a bit of the theories of Dr. Loftus, the core of her story has not changed over the years. Anto Furundzija led the accusations, led the interrogation. Anto Furundzija was present during the sexual abuse. Anto Furundzija then took me to the pantry, commenced the interrogation again. The sexual abuse started again. In, what I would call, the few times that she has been interviewed in those intervening five years, the story remains the same because that is what happened. Then, Your Honours, I would just like to speak briefly about Witness E. We thank him for coming too, a resident in the former Yugoslavia. It's obvious in Witness E's testimony that he brought forward some very good information. He, too, was frightened. He, too, was frightened probably of Accused B and, I would suggest, might have reduced his testimony in terms of Accused B. But that testimony led or tried to infer that Accused B did not brutally beat Witness D to the extent previously testified. I can understand why Witness E would want to limit it to the facts and look at his statement for 35 minutes and spend the other 18 hours in the Bungalow, I don't know, I really don't know, closing his ears, reducing his vision, having a weapon focus? But, Your Honour, Witness E places Witness D on or about May 15th in the Bungalow primed to be taken to the pantry the next morning where he would be confronted with Witness A by Anto Furundzija in the last phase of the interrogation. As I stated earlier, this case is about simple justice. This case is not that complicated in many aspects, important in several others. I would ask Your Honours to use your well-developed judicial sense to understand the testimony and the evidence. The Prosecution believes that, beyond a reasonable doubt, we have proven that Anto Furundzija, the accused who is in this courtroom today, has committed torture, has committed outrages upon personal dignity and, the very least, aided and abetted upon outrages of personal dignity, aided and abetted in the commission of rape. Your Honours, we ask this Trial Chamber to find the accused, Anto Furundzija, guilty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Your Honours. May I first say that Ms. Sellers' closing argument is framed in the form of a play, and I believe that perhaps Ms. Sellers will win an award for best fictional script. I certainly will vote for it. She said at the beginning that this was a historic case, and we agree. The case of the Prosecutor versus Anto Furundzija will be historic, in our view, because it will be the Tribunal's first acquittal. I will not try to appeal to your passions here. I will not talk about simply justice for the victim or justice for Ahmici. I'm going to talk to you about justice for all, because everyone is entitled to justice. As I said in my opening statement, the Prosecution was going to call six to eight witnesses. It turned out to be six witnesses. And other than Witness A, no one had any personal knowledge of the events in what I will refer to as the big room at the weekend house next to the Bungalow. And the only person who claimed to have any knowledge concerning the events in what will be described as the pantry, directly contradicts Witness A's version of events and, specifically, with respect to who was present in the room at the time of, I guess we'll refer to him now as, Accused B's continuing sexual and physical assaults of Witness A. Ms. Sellers' closing argument was focused very much on April 16th and on the law. I'm going to talk to you today about what the facts are and I'm going to talk to you about the events of what the Prosecution now, contrary to their opening statement says, is mid May. But first let me address the assertion that the Prosecution has proved armed conflict in this case. As you are all too familiar, it is the Prosecution's burden of proof to prove each element of the charge. And, yes, they did call many witnesses who talked about offences that were committed by Bosnian Croat forces against civilians in the Vitez municipality. However, as Mr. Blaxill stated what the law was regarding armed conflict, it is: Armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between states or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a state. I submit to you, Your Honours, that I have spent a lot of time pouring over the transcripts, and you will not find one bit of evidence that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO clashed during the relevant period. What they have shown is an attack on civilians by the HVO. They didn't tell you when that conflict between the army began. The best they could do was tell you that there were trenches dug about May 22nd, and that that is an indication that there must have been a conflict. But you will recall that when Dr. Mujezinovic testified, I made sure that in the record we included that there was conflict with the Bosnian Serbs since 1992. And he also said that the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats were on the same side fighting the Bosnian Serbs and that that main road that links Vitez and Busovaca was a communication route to the front-line against the Serbs. Now, I submit, Your Honours, that it was the Prosecution's burden to show where the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were, where HVO forces were, when this clash began, what the military objectives were. We heard none of it. What they have done is asked the court to assume or to rely on outside experience to suggest that there was an armed conflict. They failed to meet the most basic element in this case, and that is armed conflict. And it is not up to the court to fix the mistakes of the Prosecution. Now, in my opening statement, again, I told you that this case was really -- even though six witnesses would be called, that number was a facade, because the Prosecution's entire case is based on one witness, and that's Witness A. And it's not just based on her, but, specifically, it is based on her ability to recollect events, her ability to recall times, to recall dates, to recall places, sequences, people. You would have to believe in her abilities beyond a reasonable doubt if you were to convict Anto Furundzija based on her current reconstruction of events. Because, unlike most cases that you will try, there is no corroborating evidence for Witness A. None. Witness A testified that she was abducted on the 15th of May, 1993, and that she was exchanged on the 15th of August, 1993. She told you what happened to her, and we told you it was a reconstruction. Now, we know that at some point she fell into a psychological crisis in her captivity. We know that because in that second December 1993 statement, she says herself, "When I was in the weekend house in the Lasva, I would fall into psychological crisis." And that's perfectly understandable. By the time she got to Travnik after August 15th, her reconstruction of events begins out of necessity. Why? Because the people that she had known in Vitez were now refugees in Travnik or refugees in Zenica, and they all see her and they are all shocked by the sight that they see. And they say, "Witness A, tell us, what happened to you? What possibly could have happened to you?" Witness A is in no condition to be saying what happened to her. How do we know that? We know that because Dr. Mujezinovic, her physician, came in here and described her condition, mental condition, to you. She was unable to string two sentences together. She was crying all the time. She was suicidal. Dr. Mujezinovic described her as having deviated from the normal during the period of fall of 1993 through or around winter of 1994. It is this period that she is at her psychological and psychiatric low point when this reconstruction phase that Dr. Loftus described to you is taking place. In fact, it started to take place during her captivity, but certainly through this period is when her memories are being formed again, and she is potentially suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. So what happens? We have statements, we have proof that she used others to reconstruct what happened to her. In one statement, she says, "I described a man to my son, and my son said, 'Oh, yes, we recognise him. He's Josip Zuljevic. He's from the village of Krcevine.'" That's in her 1995 statement. She wanted to know at some point, "Who were those three guys that came into my apartment on the 15th of May?" Well, in one 1993 statement, she says, "Vlatko Males told my sister Dzana that it was Vujica, it was Viktor, it was Krizanac that came to pick me up." So that's what she put in her statement. Then the real serious questioning starts. At some point, a former neighbour of hers comes to visit, a next-door neighbour, someone she had known. Enes Surkovic arrives on the scene, and we talked at length with Dr. Mujezinovic about who Enes Surkovic was. Enes Surkovic was on the war presidency, and his responsibility was to take the statements of all the refugees. His responsibility, as Dr. Mujezinovic said, was to bring to justice those who had deviated from the norms of human conduct. We have testimony from Dr. Mujezinovic that in 1993, he and Mr. Surkovic had conversations about Ahmici. Not just those two. Witness C told you that the climate in Zenica at the time was that the people from Ahmici were telling their stories to everyone about what happened. The same thing was happening in Travnik at the time. People are exchanging stories, and hearsay starts to take its effect. But to get back to Enes Surkovic. Here is a man who Dr. Mujezinovic says believed that the Jokers were responsible for Ahmici. Here's a man who has a conversation with Dr. Mujezinovic not only about Accused B, but they also say, "Yes, and we know that the commander of the Jokers was Anto Furundzija," or so they believe. He had heard the stories, he knew what he needed to prove, and he knew what kind of justice, as he defines it, he wanted to mete out. So he talks to Witness A. Witness A says she didn't realise that this was going to be a statement. She described it as a conversation. Apparently -- she says it was probably in Enes Surkovic's handwriting. Apparently, Enes Surkovic forged her name to that statement. You can see the situation now. A woman who is at her low point psychologically and psychiatrically is being asked by a man who has facts, who has a purpose and a motive specifically to one man he believed was the commander of the Jokers. So what happens? A statement is written. Not by Witness A. Witness A doesn't recall ever giving a statement. She says it was a conversation. And you can imagine how that conversation went. "Neighbour, I've heard stories about you. Tell me what happened." And she can't string two sentences together. "Well, let me write it for you." She says one name, Accused B. He says, "Wasn't his boss there? It could be his boss was there, somewhere in there." And the name gets written in. Enes Surkovic had a motive to get his name in a statement. But the reconstruction doesn't end with Enes Surkovic. First of all, it turns out that the evidence is that her husband works directly below Enes Surkovic in the refugee office. Her husband certainly had the same knowledge as Enes Surkovic. There was a purpose. Her husband, the testimony indicates, knew about Ahmici because he was in the Civil Defence in Stari Vitez at the time the bodies from Ahmici were transferred and were buried by his Civil Defence. This is a man who thought he was bringing someone to justice. We have all sorts of contact now with this witness, all sorts of post-event reconstruction, suggestion as to who the important people might be to get in this statement. She herself says - she herself says - that at some point after peace, and this is in this trial testimony, after peace, presumably the Washington Accords, she talked to some of her neighbours from the area, and her neighbours said, oh, they saw who the three guys were that came to pick her up. And they weren't Dugi -- they weren't Vujica Viktor and Krizanac, they were Dugi, Sikira, and a third man. So in the 1995 statement, we have three totally different names for who came to pick her up. Why is that? Well, what happened was, somebody suggested to her that you get three different names in there, or at least two. But it doesn't end there. This was in her local community, even though it was refugees, and stories are told and people talk. But the professionals are coming. The Office of the Prosecutor for the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia now wants to talk to Witness A, and Witness A must know that this is not a forum to be telling tales, and the Prosecutor knows "We have to get this statement right because this is the statement from which indictments are going to flow." So who do they send? They send Plony Bos, an investigator, and Brenda Hollis, a Prosecutor, someone who is prosecuting in the Tadic case. They weren't going to get this wrong by sending two incompetents down to take a statement that later could be said, "It was wrong. We transcribed it wrong." They bring a translator with them. They spend two days with her. They are going to get this story straight, they are going to get the facts, they are not going to put tales on paper, as the '93 statement is, they are going to ask the questions that every investigator and Prosecutor wants to know: Who? What? When? Where? Why? How? They do it. They go through her statement very carefully, and they put it on paper. They don't want to beat around the bush. They say, "These people that you're naming, describe them. We want descriptions of these people." The descriptions are in the statement: Accused B, 190 centimetres, sturdy build, moustache; Dragan Botic, in his 40s, short, black hair, 180 centimetres; Josip Zuljevic, 22, short black hair, 170 centimetres; Anto Furundzija, 172 centimetres, blond hair, small-featured. Okay. The Prosecutors and the investigator have no knowledge as to whether those descriptions are accurate, and they believe the story. They believe it. She told them. She was sure. "April 16th; I know that date. That's the date," as she said in this courtroom, "That was the beginning of the end. How can I forget that date?" "5.45 a.m. I can tell you to the minute when it started." She says May 15th. She says May 15th in every statement she has ever given. She said May 15th on cross-examination here at least eight times. Michael Blaxill told you in his opening statement it was one horrifying day. It was May 15th. Well, now it is on or about May 15th, and what does it matter? "It is our witness and it is the same thing she has said for five years, but she's wrong." Okay. Or is she wrong? Well, we will get to that in a minute. This statement is used to bring indictments, and an indictment is filed and confirmed in November of 1995. The Prosecutors and investigators were led to believe a story which appeared to be seamless. All of these events seem to fit into place. Everything happened in one day. Again, opening statement: "It is one horrific day. That's what this case is about." "The case," he said, "is focused on the events of one day, 15 May, 1993." He described it in the opening as: In the morning, she's taken, she's taken to the big room, Anto Furundzija arrives shortly thereafter, all sorts of heinous crimes are committed in his presence while he is interrogating. He is not getting the answers he wants, so he gets upset. He leaves. He takes her to the pantry. And this is a continuation. A "second phase," as he described it. Witness A testified exactly as Mr. Blaxill told you she would. It was 15 May and it was one day. Contrary to the claim there, there was no continuation on 15 May. There was no second phase. You know, here we are talking very much about witness memory, witness testimony, no corroboration. If only we had demonstrative evidence to check these people's memories, to check their accuracy. Well, the Defence did provide demonstrative evidence for the Trial Chamber. We showed you Defence Exhibit 10. We showed you that Witness D could not have come out of Stari Vitez until at least 16 May, 1993. To make their theory of the case work when we started, he had to have been released on 13 May, because you will recall, his testimony is: "I didn't see Witness A until the third day of my captivity." So he had to be out on the 13th of May. Well, if Witness A testifies, and she is their witness, if she says she was taken on 15 May, and now the evidence is she couldn't possibly have been in the pantry until May 18th or, as Witness E said, they were taken to the Bungalow on the 17th, on May 19th she was taken to the pantry. Now, the Prosecution wants you to just think, "Oh, what does it matter what day it was?" Well, it matters for this reason. The question is: Was it one day? Witness A testified consistently she was taken to the pantry on 15 May. Mr. Blaxill said she was taken to the -- excuse me, to the house on 15 May. She says, "I remember dates. I remember 16 April. I remember 5.45 a.m. " I asked her, "Do you remember the time of day you were taken on 15 May?" "Absolutely. I was taken at 10.30 because I picked up my watch, and I remember looking at my watch and it was 10.30 in the morning." So how do we square this? Well, it is interesting to look back on her testimony because now she says she only spent one day at that weekend house next to the Bungalow. But that is not what she has always said. In 1993, in two statements, she says, "I spent three days there." She spent three days there. Now, that is consistent with some of the testimony she has given. She has combined three or four days of events into one day and made it all 15 May in her head, the day she was taken. She also gets other things confused. She says in 1995, on the next day, she was taken to the weekend house by the Lasva where she spent the rest of her time. Here, she raised a new issue. She said, "Oh, no, no, no, no, no. The next day, I was taken to Accused B's house where I spent a couple of days." She said that on my cross-examination. "The next day I was taken to Accused B's house." Let's look at that day that she describes. 10.30 in the morning, she's taken. She arrives in the big room. She says she's repeatedly sexually assaulted and raped in the big room in front of soldiers. Then she says, "And then, at some point, I'm left alone with Accused B, and he assaults me and rapes me and then he falls asleep, and then he assaults me and rapes me and then he falls asleep, and assaults me and rapes me and falls asleep. And then I was taken to the pantry and then I went to the Lasva house (redacted) (redacted)"

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: matter of two or three hours on the afternoon of one day in the life. She has crammed days where he kept her locked up, would fall asleep, wake up, go about his business, come back. These are days of events. That is why 15 May is significant and can't be brushed aside. What we also know is, Ms. Sellers is wrong when she says the evidence is uncontroverted that Mr. Furundzija was there from the beginning. It is controverted by her own witness. In 1995, to the Prosecutor, to Plony Bos under oath, repeated back to her, she says, "I was taken to the big room. Some other young men, who I can't identify, started to ask me questions. Accused B jumped up behind me, grabbed me by the hair, put a knife to my throat, caressed my body with a knife, and then started to sexually assault and rape me. And there were other soldiers in the room. Then they left, and he continued on alone." "And then what happened?" "Well, then the boss arrived. He did not ask me what had happened to

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: someone who is in a rage, as the Prosecution wishes to suggest, have to ask her or the perpetrator what had happened? It is contradicted by their own witness. If they want to come back and say, "Now she's saying something different," well, is that a witness you can rely on beyond a reasonable doubt? Now, let's get to the heart of the case because I am going to talk to you about the heart of the case and I am not going to just skip over it, and that's the pantry. I told you she was going to come into this room and she was going to sit in that chair and she was going to be confident and she was going to be sure of herself and she was going to tell you a story, and I also told you she was going to be wrong. Now, I confronted her with that statement, that 1995 statement. I asked her a series of questions, went through it. "You said this: You described him as 172 centimetres and blond." She doesn't deny making the statement. She says, "Sir," that's what she said to me, "Sir, I'm the victim. I know what happened. I was there." I'm not going to argue with the victim, but I have to, because she was also the victim and she was also the one that was there in 1995 when she was talking to the Prosecutor and she was talking to the investigator; and you have to use her testimony to see whether you believe it beyond a reasonable doubt, whether she is so reliable that her testimony, uncorroborated, can convict a man of rape and torture. She looked you right in the eye, she looked me right in the eye, and she said, "Anto Furundzija was present in the pantry interrogating me while both "D" and I were being beaten and while I was being raped by Accused B." Not only that, but she said, "So there's no mistake about this, the questioning and the sexual assault and rape were parallel." Indeed, Ms. Sellers asked her a question, which ultimately got stricken, but she said, "So depending on the answer, did the intensity of the sexual assault increase?" And the question was stricken. But that is evidence that there was no mistake about what she meant. Furundzija was there, Furundzija is asking questions, and depending upon her answer, she is being raped. She was confident and she was wrong. Why do we know she was wrong? Well, Witness D comes into the courtroom, a Prosecution witness, a man apparently with no love loss for Mr. Furundzija, and he told you that. The Prosecution's own witness told you that. He said, "I was taken on the 16th, and it wasn't until the third day of my presence in the Bungalow that I was taken over to the weekend house next to the Bungalow." And he says "I walked," and he doesn't say Anto Furundzija took him to the pantry, he says, "I got downstairs in the Bungalow, Anto Furundzija was standing around, and Accused B, Anto Furundzija, and a bunch of other soldiers walked to the other house." And then he says, "they" walked in the room. He doesn't say who. He says, "When I got to the room, Witness A was already there. She was in the room ." But Witness A testified, "Somebody came in the room, and Accused B and another individual came and took me, and I turned the corner and I brushed Mr. Furundzija's elbow." And who is in the room, but Witness D? I think Dr. Loftus's testimony helps us here, or at least is proven by this point. Two people come into this courtroom and say, "I walked into the room and the other one was already there." The other one comes in and says, "No, I walked into the room, and the other one was already there." Again, her ability to recollect faces, times, dates, et cetera. What else does Witness D tell you? "Well, I started to get hit, and I got hit first. Then after Accused B was done with me, then he turned his attention to 'A'." Okay. So the Prosecution asks, "All right. While you were being beaten in that first part, was anybody else in the room?" "No." "Well, did you see anyone around?" "Yes. Outside the door, I could see a group of soldiers." Okay. "So they're outside the door. Could you identify anyone?" "Yeah. One of them was Anto Furundzija." Okay. So then the question is asked: "Well, how many times did you see him there?" The question being asked to see whether he was there for the entire incident. And he says, "You know what? I don't know. I looked up once, I saw him there, but I can't tell you at what point that was." Mm-hmm. "Well, did they know what was going on?" He believes so. In other words, "I guess so. I don't know." He believes so. He guesses so. This sounds like a man who is an active participant, who is in such a rage, as Ms. Sellers describes him, that one of the people that is being beaten can't even come in here and tell you for sure whether he was around when this was going on? Another important element is: He's asked, "Okay. What happened when you left the room? Did you see anyone?" "No." "Okay. Well, you were taken out of the house, right?" "Yeah." "And you were taken back to the bungalow?" "Yes." "Well, did you see anyone on your way back to the Bungalow?" "No." Most importantly: "Did you see Anto Furundzija?" "No." Ms. Sellers talks about, he heard screaming at some point that night. Let's look at Witness A's testimony. Witness A never says she screamed. Witness A says, "I was like a stone. I couldn't move. I couldn't do anything." So the accusation that Furundzija was around someplace while this woman was screaming contradicts Witness A's own testimony. In fact, it contradicts Witness D who says, on Judge Cassese's questioning, "No, she wasn't screaming." "Well, was she crying loudly?" "No, she wasn't crying loudly." Witness A is wrong. She's very wrong. She has accused a man of being an active participant, of conducting an interrogation while she is being raped and beaten, and we have a Prosecution witness who says she has got her facts very, very wrong. I can't imagine a bigger mistake. But this is not the first time that "A" has falsely accused someone of raping her in the pantry. Recall that in 1993, she said basically she was gang-raped. "They took turns raping me, about five or six of them, in the pantry."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: She says at some point in the pantry -- I don't recall now whether she said it was Mr. Furundzija or somebody else – (redacted) guitar to make it more of a party atmosphere. Okay? Well, that's not what she said when she testified in another case before this Tribunal. She said, "No, no, that guitar-playing was back in the big room early on." In every other statement, including her testimony here, she says, "No, it was in the pantry." But Witness D is here, and Witness D doesn't describe anything like people coming in and playing guitar. He can't even tell you whether people knew what was going on outside, that were standing outside, and how long they were there. He doesn't know that. Again, memory, the fragility of memory. The susceptibility to influence from outsiders. Witness D told you a lot about Witness A's memory. His testimony allows you to see how reliable Witness A is. His testimony allows you to see whether Anto Furundzija conducted an interrogation in the pantry during the rapes and beatings. His testimony confirms what we said in our opening statement, that Witness A has it wrong, Witness A's reconstruction is not reliable, let alone convincing beyond a reasonable doubt. Not only does the Prosecution fail to bring any corroborating evidence for her testimony, but they call a witness who impeaches their own star witness. But it is not too difficult to see why she has a problem trying to place Anto Furundzija. In 1995, again, her Anto Furundzija was 172 centimetres, blond hair, small-featured. In 1998, her Anto Furundzija is 180 centimetres, chestnut brown to black hair, and a strong jaw. Not small features. Well, forgive me if I ask the court to take judicial notice that he has a rather large nose too. Now, we have introduced the medical record this morning. Anto Furundzija is 183 centimetres tall, brown to black hair, prominent features. She made an 11-centimetre mistake, mistake as to hair, mistake as to features, and Witness E told you, when I asked, "Is there somebody around the Bungalow in the period of 15 May through 18 May that fit the description of 172 centimetres and blond hair?" "Yes, two people." She is wrong about this. She can't identify him. Interestingly enough, the Prosecution's star witness is called to the stand. The Prosecution completes its entire questioning of Witness A and never asks her to identify the accused. It was only because Judge Mumba asked the question that there was ever an identification. Now, the Tadic court is on record as saying in-court identifications are not very worthwhile. Indeed, most of the witnesses in this case described Mr. Furundzija as the man sitting next to the armed soldier, uniformed, and he is the only man who is either not in a uniform or in a robe in the courtroom. Yet they didn't ask her to identify him. So Judge Mumba then asks, and she identifies him without problem. Now the Defence starts to ask questions about the key witness's ability to identify the accused, to ask her questions about her 1995 description, and the Prosecution objects, objects to any line of questioning about an identification by the victim of the Defendant. We suggest, Your Honours, that a reasonable inference can be drawn that Witness A was not able to identify the Defendant. If Witness A is wrong about this, if she can't identify him, if she is wrong about the date, if she is wrong about the guitar, if she is grossly wrong about the pantry, how can you believe her beyond a reasonable doubt? She talks about, or the Prosecution talks about, an interrogation. Anto Furundzija, professional interrogator. That's his role in the play described by Ms. Sellers. The play makes no sense, based on this evidence. None. Why? The theory is the HVO, or Anto Furundzija and the Jokers, knew about this relationship between "D" and "A" and, as Ms. Sellers said in her closing, "And this was professional. This was about getting names of people that she was working with in the HVO," et cetera, et cetera. Okay. Let's pursue that line of thinking. So we have Witness D, she is taken to the big room, she is asked questions. The theory is, because she is not answering correctly the questions, she starts to be beaten, she is threatened with a knife, she is sexually assaulted, she is raped because she is giving the wrong answers. The theory is that it is about Witness A and her contacts with others. Okay. So I asked Witness A, I said, "Okay. During this whole period before your entry into the pantry, did anybody ask you if you knew Witness D?" "Oh, no." "Wait a minute. They're beating you because of your relationship, the assistance that "D" gave you on the 16th, you're not giving the right answers, but nobody bothered to say, 'Oh, by the way, Witness A, do you know Witness D?'" Even more interesting, she gets to the pantry and she says right away, "Oh, yeah, I know him. (redacted) (redacted)."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the law and the Tadic decision which is relevant to this case. The Prosecution must prove an intent to participate, an awareness of the act of participation. Witness D has no idea. He says he was outside the room I don't know when. I don't know at what point he was outside the room. I don't even know whether he knew what was going on in the room. Is that an intent to participate? The next step is participation. The conduct of the accused contributed to the commission of the illegal act. First, again, there is no proof that he was there for any of this. There is no proof that he ever said or did anything, other than Witness A's reconstruction. Another element is there must be some overt act or omission. The Tadic court said there must be participation. For even if a man is present whilst a felony is committed, if he takes no part in it and does not act in concert with those who commit it, he will not be a principal in the second degree merely because he did not endeavour to prevent it. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: (redacted)." That seems to be stretching for duality, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: (redacted). There is no credible evidence that he was outside the pantry during the sexual assault of Witness A or her rape or her beating. Witness D says he looked up and saw him there but doesn't recall when, and Anto Furundzija was not around when he left the room. Again, Your Honours, you were told in my opening statement that the Prosecution's entire case rested on one witness. It rests on Witness A, and it rests on her ability to recollect events. You would have to find that her memory is so convincing, is so accurate, that based on her reconstruction alone, you are convinced beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of Anto Furundzija. Well, Your Honours, we have seen that Witness A's memory has failed her many times on many significant events. Perhaps the Prosecution, in rebuttal, can answer some of these questions: When did it happen? Was it May 15th? Was it all in one day or was it three days? Who is the 172-centimetre, blond-haired, small-featured man? When did Zuljevic play the guitar, at the pantry, as she said here, or in the big room, as she said in 1997 trial testimony? Who brought her to the pantry? Was it Accused B, Anto Furundzija and Dugi, as she said in 1995? Or was it Accused B and another man and not Furundzija, as she said here? Who was in the pantry first? Was "D" in the pantry first or was "A" in the pantry first? When was she taken to the house by the Lasva? This time, for the first time, she says she was taken there on that day. That's something new. Now she was at the house at the Lasva on that day and then taken back. And then the next day, she was taken to Accused B's house. Was she taken to the house on the Lasva the next day, as she said in 1995? Was she taken two days later, as she said in 1993? You know, the Prosecution got up in their closing argument and said, "Well, she's got the core right." Well, first of all, no, she doesn't. She has the date wrong. She has the ID wrong. She has the pantry wrong. If that's not the core of a case against an accused, I don't know what is. But what does that say about your witness? The witness that your whole case rests on, you tell the court, "Okay, so she makes some mistakes. Okay, so she's wrong a couple of times, but there's been some things that she's been consistent about." That, to me, cannot be a witness that you can rely on uncorroborated beyond a reasonable doubt. Such a huge, terrible mistake as the pantry must create reasonable doubt in your minds about this case. If she could falsely accuse Anto Furundzija of being a direct participant in her rape, she can be mistaken about anything, and the reasons are clear. At the time of her memory formation, she was a psychiatric patient who was being visited by people with a motive, by one person, in particular, Enes Surkovic. This is a case, Your Honours, that has not only reasonable doubt, it has reasonable doubts. This is the case that cries out for an acquittal. The Prosecution has failed miserably to meet their burden of proof. Your Honours, the Defence asks you to enter an order acquitting Anto Furundzija. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to find out from the Prosecution whether they have anything in rebuttal to reply to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the word would be certain matters I would wish to offer you in rebuttal, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, how long do you think you will take? It's past lunch-hour now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, yes, I would imagine 15, 20 minutes, maybe a little longer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In that case, then we will sit in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. I certainly don't expect to be much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam President, I just wish to alert you that we also may wish to have rebuttal after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, the court will adjourn and sit this afternoon at 14.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We continue with closing arguments and rebuttal by the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am obliged. I hope everyone can hear clearly. Your Honours, I do have just a few points I would like to make in rebuttal of the points made in the closing address by the Defence. The first issue being that of the adequacy of evidence of armed conflict. You have heard from principally Dr. Mujezinovic and from Mr. Kavazovic, and you have heard, in the course of their evidence in chief, which, as I understand, went unchallenged by the Defence, that certainly from April of 1993, there was clear evidence of conflict, not just attack on civilian population by the HVO but also from the evidence of Kavazovic, who was arrested in late April '93 and was taken to the lines to dig trenches, that when he got there, there was active firing between two established lines of armies, the ABH and the HVO, and that he worked initially under the bullets, as it were, flying between the two parties. Both of those then gave the ongoing evidence relating to the continuation of the conflict through and beyond the period of mid-May, and you have heard how both eventually heard about peace negotiations, at the very least, and in the case of Mr. Kavazovic, an eventual order for general cease-fire. I suggest that with the detail given by Dr. Mujezinovic as to events, as to Mr. Kavazovic's observations as a serving soldier, and, indeed, then the anecdotal, if you like, evidence of the two ladies, Witnesses B and C, as to the conditions prevailing, that the existence of a situation of armed conflict I respectfully suggest, is an inescapable conclusion. There has been reference also to the question of dates, lack of precision as to dates, and it is clear that when it was -- if you look at the indictment, the initial pleading is "on or about the 15th of May." Now, one can polarise on a date, but it has been pleaded to be bracketing the specific date, and indeed several of the witnesses have made reference to the fact that they are weak on specific dates, one of them confirming that a date is hard to remember in terms of the prevailing conditions that they had in their community at the time. Many were saying, "Well, it was on or about" or "It was a few days before," or "I was there six, eight, or ten days. I'm not sure." I think this is a common thread and one which Your Honours may feel is an understandable common thread amongst people who were living through those times and those conditions. In point of fact, Witness A never volunteered any information as to the date. My learned friend, Ms. Sellers, actually asked her about what happened to her in "mid-May," and the only references thereafter in the course of her testimony, to the best of my recollection, were when counsel for the Defence would state to her, "And on the 15th of May, what time were you arrested?" or "At what hour did this happen?" or "What happened on the 15th of May?" rather than any question of asking her to confirm "Was it indeed the 15th of May?" I think if you examine the transcript, the answers went to the substance of the question after the date, not confirming the date itself. I would suggest, Your Honours, that in such circumstances as appertained, some, let us use the word "woolliness" as to dates by people involved is not inconsistent with true recollection of events that took place. It is a question, really, of consistency. You have heard numerous suggestions of inconsistency in the various hypotheses that my learned friend, Mr. Misetic, has put to you, but there are certain quite concrete consistencies, if you like, that give a logic to the events, and these, I think, are the most telling features and factors of the case. We have a situation where, initially, Witness D speaks to his arrest on a given date, a date, in fact, documented, and that document is not disputed. Subsequently, Witness E is arrested and informed by the people arresting him, the same people, Jokers, that they "already had D in their hands." When arriving at the Bungalow, the Defence witness himself, Witness E, states that he saw Witness D present. He saw some of the beating of Witness D. He particularly noted the manner in which the feet were beaten. That is repeated. That is repeated by Witness A and Witness D in the incident in the pantry, the manner, the perhaps unusual or distinctive manner, in which the feet of these people were beaten. I suggest that the evidence of Witness E alone lends credibility to Witness D stating how long he was at the Bungalow, the fact that he says he spent two nights there, and it was then on the third, I take the first day as being the day of arrest, the third day that the confrontation took place. The Jokers by then had arrested Witness A, and one can ask one simple logical question: Unless there had been something in their minds, in the minds of the interrogators, to "B," the interrogator in chief, if there was not something in his mind as to a link between "D" and "A", what on earth would be the point of these two people being arrested and being placed in the confrontation? It would be meaningless. So I suggest that those very circumstances show that clearly, when Witness A was arrested and brought in, Witness D was already there, and that the link between them was already known to those who would be speaking to Witness A. The interrogation proceeds, and you have heard a clear identification that the interrogator was the man who came in, referred to as Furundzija, a man who Witness A then said her various questions, pertinent types of questions, about her two sons of military age. She does have two sons who then were of military age. Questions about persons she knew and persons she may have had contact with within the community. This interrogation was clearly, I would suggest from that evidence, a logical -- we're following a course of logic from evidence which is largely uncontested and is a matter, I suggest, of concrete fact. If we then take it forward, we have Witness D who is brought in. And, indeed, who is part of the group bringing him in? It is the same Mr. Furundzija, a Mr. Furundzija whom Witness A has said has been her interrogator. The confrontation, she alleges, was threatened by him; and is she not right in that contention? Is this some kind of imposed memory or factual scenario that she has subsequently acquired? I would suggest not, Your Honours. I would suggest not, because, again, why would she be there? Why would "D" be there? Why would this confrontation take place? The reality is they suspected "D" of being essentially a traitor, and they suspected him of helping the Muslims, and he had aided Witness A. Taking that scenario forward, we then have the situation. And this is not where I'm trying to pick random facts to say, "Oh, here is an inconsistency; therefore, the story is untrue or badly recollected or rolled through various psychological pressures." I'm following the logic as I see it, Your Honours, of the way the evidence has panned out. In that room, "D" and "A" are present together. They recognise each other. The condition of "D" is described by "A"; the condition of "A" described by "D." She is deeply upset; she is crying; she is naked, bar a small blanket. And he in turn, "D", looks badly beaten to her quite, sort of, shocking condition. There is clear evidence that if that observation would reflect the allegations that are made about previous events, what "D" has said about his treatment by the other man in the Bungalow, and her treatment in the larger room prior to being taken to that pantry. That is consistent, Your Honours. It is consistent. Then she describes the events that took place, and here we go to what was another -- originally, as I understand it, the challenge that was put to Witness A in response to Your Honour, Judge May. What was the challenge that was put, and Mr. Misetic put his challenge, that "Whatever happened to you in that room, Mr. Furundzija wasn't present." This, perhaps, is the real issue here, is it? I know not. But we say that Mr. Furundzija is the interrogator. He's arranged the confrontation. This confrontation is not some kind of time warp event that stops the clock dead on what has happened before, and then we move on anew with something different. This is something which occurs in the course of the events of the interrogation. Two parties are brought in. The confrontation takes place. Witness A recalls questions being asked. That may be disputed, but the comment by the Defence, I understand, was that here is a lady who is not corroborated but, indeed, contradicted by Witness D. I'm not so sure that that is a contradiction. Your Honours, Witness D may have had reasons. He's a young Bosnian Croat. He may have had reasons to be a little cautious in how much he said about one of his own kind who is on trial, but the fact of the matter is this: He does not recall and he said, "I did not hear Furundzija asking questions," but he did say that Mr. Furundzija was in the doorway area. He made reference to his presence with the other Jokers just outside the room, just outside the room, a room that was described as small, the events going on in front of an open door a very short distance from that doorway. Therefore, I suggest that that is not pure contradiction of Witness A. He cannot say for sure one way or the other whether Mr. Furundzija spoke questions at that time. That does not mean that Witness A does not recall correctly or that she is not accurate or truthful in what she has said. Then we go through the quite horrendous description of what the Defence have just referred to, that perhaps this man, let's call him Accused B, Accused B on a rampage. Well, one wonders what rampage this man would have, what motivation he would have vis-à-vis Witness A, since apparently, if he had a motive at all, it would be some kind of punishment of Witness D for, I think the expression used was, for ratting him out. The bottom line, Your Honours, is that we have, in fact, corroboration here in the main. Witness D corroborates, I suggest, far more than he, in any way, not so much contradicts, but certainly may not have recalled every detail. If two witnesses do not recall every detail, does that not speak to the potential truth of their recollections and the truth of their stories? Two people who come before a courtroom and almost verbatim echo each other do not necessarily mean that they are highly credible. It is sometimes the small differences, the differences in perspective, the differences in their level of recollection, which speak to the truth of the circumstances. Your Honours, it's been suggested that, therefore, the lady, Witness A, despite this scenario, despite these small areas of fact which give considerable bolster to the concept of what has really happened here, we are then invited to say, "Well, in fact, this is all due to memory being implanted later," she has suffered this and that, and as a result we have a lady whose recollections sadly, despite the tragedy affecting her, her recollections are totally unreliable. Your Honours, I would take issue with that on the basis that, with respect, the expert evidence you've heard is very much general, was expressed to be so, and Dr. Loftus confirmed that she had had a conversation with the Defence lawyers. She had skimmed a couple of statements. She had absolutely no personal, clinical, experimental or in-depth study of anything, documents, people, or the case at all. And she has to apply simply some very general principles. Her examples included things like two-minute and 15-second film clips used in a controlled way with experimental people to gauge reaction. I think there is a considerable difference between that kind of scenario and the reality of what this case represents in terms of the time, the time span of the events happening to Witness A, to Witness D, and also to the elements such as, I think the expression was, "core details." The identification of your interrogator, if you are going to focus, surely, on such an event, things of significance would be who is the investigator, who is that person asking you the questions, and also who is that person, perhaps, pressing a knife against you? They would both be core details you would remember. The number of windows in the wall, how many other people present might be peripheral information you might not be so sure of. But I would suggest that, to use Dr. Loftus's concept, these would be core details in respect of which there is certainty on the part of witnesses. I will go to essentially my last point, Your Honours, and that is this: When we come to the identification of Mr. Furundzija, we have an abundance of identification. It appears pretty much undisputed from the facts that he was a member of the Jokers, he worked at the Bungalow, he worked out of the Bungalow. His role was variously described but, in the main, the witnesses felt he had some situation of authority. He appeared, if he carried out an interrogation, that would indicate that to be so. But the main thing was each and every one person who was invited to look around this courtroom unhesitatingly identified the man, Mr. Furundzija; and what is more - and what is more - it is suggested that he was identified because he is sitting next to the uniformed man. In fact, as I recall each witness, their initial response was to refer to Mr. Furundzija as the man in the suit wearing a tie with dark hair, with headphones, whatever, and then a couple, I believe, stated "Sitting next to the man in the blue uniform shirt." There is no evidence, no evidence put forward in this case, Your Honours, that Mr. Furundzija was planted in the mind of Witness A, and that is another factor I would ask you to consider very carefully. Nothing has been suggested that somebody came along and said, "Mr. Furundzija was the man who ..." The evidence does not bear out that suggestion. As a result, what I think is so telling in this case is that two people have come together to give evidence in this court some four years from the time they last met and largely corroborating each other as to facts, without, as I believe, they confirmed in evidence, without any contact over those four years. It would be, would it not, stretching credulity to believe that these two people could have had their recollections so repressed, so altered, or so suggested by outside forces that they are both so totally mistaken? I honestly cannot believe that to be the case. Those are the representations that I have to make, Your Honours. I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything in rebuttal -- in rejoinder, rather?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In rejoinder, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. A few points, Your Honours. First, let me address the comments of Mr. Blaxill. The argument here from the Defence with respect to the date has nothing to do with whether it was pleaded properly in the indictment, it has to do with Witness A's memory. It has to do with not just her memory but whether this was a single continuation one day or whether it was over the course of three days. I posed the question before we broke as to whether the Prosecution could explain why, five years of claims by Witness A -- forget about what is in the indictment -- Witness A for five years has said it happened on the 15th of May. The statement that she never confirmed that is also incorrect. She volunteered that herself. I refer the court to the trial transcript of the cross-examination of Witness A to page 460, the question begins on line 15. It is quite a long question. To shorten it, I'll say, "... 'Dragan told me they were taking me to this weekend house and that someone would come to take me home.'" The answer is: "It was that day, the 15th of April." And then she corrected herself a little bit later on. So the statement that she never volunteered that in this courtroom is incorrect. Secondly, the Prosecution makes a big deal about the fact that people have confirmed that Witness D had his feet beaten with a baton. Yes, they have that confirmed and they have it confirmed that it was by Accused B, and what that has to do with whether Mr. Furundzija was ever present during any of this escapes me. Third, with respect to the questioning, again, the Prosecution has no answer. Witness A, now says Mr. Blaxill, was brought to the Bungalow because of her supposed relationship with Witness D. Why? It makes no logic. I mean, I put the question directly to Witness A. "This whole period in the big room that you were there, did anybody ask you if you knew Witness D?"
