And she said "No." She would have readily given her response because we know she did right after that. As soon as she was brought to the pantry, someone asked her, "Do you know him?" And she said "Yes." It's inexplicable to me. It leads to the conclusion, the inescapable conclusion, that this was done by Mr. Bralo. Now, Mr. Blaxill poses the question: "What is the motivation for Accused B?" Well, let me ask: What is the motivation for Accused B when Mr. Kavazovic is digging trenches to put a pickaxe next to someone's head and threaten them if they don't perform the sign of the cross properly? I believe my colleague knows full well that Accused B is not, or was not at the time, a rational person and was apparently -- and I can base this on the evidence -- known to excess. So why would he rape Witness A? He raped Witness A because it was his modus operandi. Making Muslim prisoners cross themselves, all sorts of atrocities that are attributed to him. So there is no logic as to why he would want to rape someone. Core details. Mr. Blaxill says, "Well, wouldn't Witness A remember core details, like who was interrogating me, who was threatening me, et cetera?" Well, doesn't the same apply to Witness D? Witness A says Witness D was in the room being questioned by Furundzija. If this is such a core detail that wouldn't be forgotten, why wouldn't Witness D remember this? Why wouldn't Witness D corroborate this and say, "You know what? This was a joint production between Accused B and Mr. Furundzija," and they were both in the room and, as Witness A said, parallel questioning, rapes and beatings, et cetera. There is no evidence of that other than Witness A's recollection. Witness D directly contradicts that. I cannot emphasise that point enough, and I will explain later why I don't think that is really a point in controversy here. Is there evidence that this name was planted? Yes, there is evidence that this name was planted. The evidence is, it was put to her in July of 1995, "Who is Anto Furundzija? Describe him." She missed badly. That's the evidence of why this is a plant. She never knew Anto Furundzija. And then Brenda Hollis and Plony Bos come in and say, "Give us an ID then." "Now, there's a problem, because I don't really remember what he looks like." So he's a 172-centimetre blond-haired man with small features. "Oh, but then in December of 1997, I see a BBC picture. I see now what he is. Black hair, strong jaw." She saw the head shot. That's the evidence that this was a plant because she couldn't identify him. You don't need to take my word for in-court identifications. I simply refer you to the opinion and judgement in the Tadic case with respect to what the Trial Chamber found about the reliability of in-court identifications. I said in my opening statement, "Confidence is not a barometer of reliability." May 15th is important. May 15th is one of those things that she said, "This is absolutely the day it happened." Now, if they're saying she's wrong about the date, then they're saying their own witness is wrong. If they are saying she's right about the date, then it couldn't have all happened on one day and, most importantly, she's wrong about the pantry. I cannot emphasise something enough. Their own witness says, "No, it didn't happen this way." How can a witness come in and say, Witness A, in particular, "This is the man who was interrogating me, questioning me. Every time I gave the wrong response, the rapes would continue on," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. And another person in the small room, as Mr. Blaxill describes it, who is there says, "You know, I don't remember things that way." Your Honours, Witness D, had we called him in our case in chief, could not have testified better. He could have, actually, but the point is, if she can get something wrong like that, then, Your Honours, you cannot rely on her beyond a reasonable doubt. Let's look at this case now since it's at its conclusion and this issue that Witness D is now a corroborating witness. As you are well aware, the 1995 statement was the statement upon which this entire case was based. You've read the indictment as many times as I have, if not more. The initial sexual assault, the beatings, the interrogation, et cetera, in the big room was alleged in the indictment to have occurred outside of Mr. Furundzija's presence. Any suggestion now that that's not the case is a bit disingenuous, because if he were in the room, I would imagine that the Prosecution would have filed Counts 9, 10 and 11 against Mr. Furundzija too. But that's what the 1995 statement said, and that's not what they believed. So what happens then in the meantime? Well, Witness A testifies in another case, and she totally puts Mr. Furundzija in a different location. Now he's there from the beginning. So what to do? Well, they continue on with the theory that this is a pantry case. That's confirmed in pleadings filed here, most specifically, the Prosecutor's response to the 29 April, 1998 order. It is unmistakable that the Prosecutor, as of that date, as of May 1, actually, thought that Anto Furundzija arrived after Accused B had done all of this. They filed a pre-trial brief towards the middle of May, I don't recall the exact date, saying the same thing. So what happened between the middle of May and this case to now to say, "All right. Now he's there at the beginning." What happened was Witness D was interviewed and Witness D did not corroborate the pantry any more. So what to do? You shift the spotlight off the pantry, you make him present in the big room, and you say the pantry is a second phase. It's a continuation, because now you know you have a direct contradiction. That's the way you try to make this case work. But it doesn't work, because Witness D puts him outside of the room, and Witness A has been directly contradicted. It's unmistakable. Your Honours, I have just a couple of more remarks in closing. The standard at this Tribunal is beyond a reasonable doubt. If I may just say this to you: If behind me today were sitting Accused B and he was sitting in that chair, and based on the evidence that you have heard in this case, you would have heard the testimony of Witness A; you would have had the corroborating testimony against him of Witness D; you would have had Witness E who said this was his modus operandi, beating on the feet, that he was in a rage for some period of time; I suggest to you that you would not have to exit that door today to have been convinced already beyond a reasonable doubt of his guilt. You wouldn't have to leave this room to have already come to that conclusion. I don't think you can say the same about Anto Furundzija. If you have to go back to your chambers and start pouring over the transcripts to try to figure out ways as to whether Anto Furundzija could have been in a particular place or could not have been, then I suggest to you that you already have a reasonable doubt about this case. Your Honours, again, the Defence respectfully requests you to enter an order acquitting Anto Furundzija. And we thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much to all the parties. This is the close of the case in this case of the Prosecutor versus Anto Furundzija. The Trial Chamber will adjourn and consider the issues before the Trial Chamber. And the date for judgement will be provided to the parties in due course. The court will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
